item.title: Preparing Almond Production for European Markets
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Producers approaching European markets for the first time often treat compliance as a final step — get the crop, then find out what the buyer needs. That sequence does not work for tree nuts, because the requirements that matter are determined years earlier by decisions in the orchard and in the design of the processing facility.

By the time a consignment exists, most of its compliance status is already fixed.

Maximum residue levels

The EU sets maximum residue levels for pesticide active substances in food. For almonds, as for everything else, a consignment exceeding an MRL cannot be sold.

What makes this an upstream issue:

Approved substances differ between jurisdictions. A product legally registered and routinely used in the producing country may have no EU MRL, or a very low default one. Using it during the season disqualifies the crop, and there is no processing step that removes it.

The spray programme is the compliance mechanism. MRL compliance is achieved by choosing substances with EU MRLs, observing pre-harvest intervals, and applying at approved rates. That is a planning decision made before the season, not a testing decision made after.

Application accuracy matters. Over-application, poor calibration or spray drift between blocks can produce residues above the level the programme intended. Sprayer calibration is a compliance activity.

Records are the evidence. Every application — product, rate, date, block, operator, weather — recorded contemporaneously. An audit will ask, and reconstruction after the fact is neither convincing nor reliable.

Practical requirement: design the spray programme against the EU MRL list for the target market before the season starts, and verify that every product in the store has an EU MRL for almonds.

Aflatoxin

The requirement that carries the most risk, because it is a food-safety limit rather than a marketing standard and the EU limits for tree nuts are strict.

Aflatoxins are produced by Aspergillus species growing on the nut. Growth requires moisture and time. Control is therefore entirely about preventing the conditions, because there is no treatment that removes aflatoxin from a contaminated batch — contaminated product is condemned.

The control points, in order of occurrence:

Harvest timing. Nuts left too long on the tree or on the orchard floor, particularly after rain, are exposed to conditions that favour fungal growth. Hull split with delayed harvest is a specific risk.

Time from harvest to drying. The critical interval. Product waiting in the field, in trailers, or in a queue at the facility is product at risk. This is why receiving and drying capacity — not shelling capacity — determines how fast harvest can safely run.

Drying to a safe moisture content, and verifying it. Measured, recorded, and to a specification, not judged by appearance.

Storage conditions. Moisture and temperature controlled, and monitored. Product correctly dried and then stored where it can reabsorb moisture is back at risk.

Insect damage control. Damaged kernels are entry points for fungal infection.

Sorting. Removing visibly damaged, discoloured and mouldy kernels reduces the load. Optical sorting is increasingly the standard. Sorting reduces risk; it does not substitute for the earlier steps.

Sampling and testing. Aflatoxin distribution in a lot is extremely heterogeneous — contamination may be concentrated in a very small proportion of kernels. This makes sampling protocol critical: a small or badly drawn sample can easily miss contamination that is present, or find contamination that is unrepresentative. Follow the prescribed sampling methodology rather than an informal version of it.

The design implication: drying capacity and speed are food-safety infrastructure. Specifying a facility around shelling throughput because that is the number people quote, and treating drying as ancillary, builds in a permanent aflatoxin risk.

See Almond Processing and Export Development.

Traceability

EU food law requires that food be traceable through the supply chain. In practice, a buyer or auditor will expect you to identify, for any consignment, which blocks it came from, when they were harvested, how the product was processed and when, where it was stored, and what test results apply to it.

This has to be designed into operations:

  • Lot identity maintained through processing. The point at which product from different blocks is combined is the point at which traceability granularity is fixed. Combining early is operationally simpler and traceably coarser — and if a problem is found, the recall scope is whatever you combined.
  • Records at every transfer between field, transport, receiving, drying, storage and dispatch.
  • A documented system, not institutional memory.

The commercial argument for granular traceability is risk containment. Fine lot separation means a problem affects a small quantity. Coarse separation means it affects everything it was mixed with.

Hygiene and facility standards

Buyers will expect a documented food-safety management system based on HACCP principles, and most European retail buyers will require certification to a recognised scheme (BRCGS, IFS, FSSC 22000 or similar).

This is a facility design matter as much as a procedural one — layout that separates clean and dirty processes, surfaces and equipment that can be cleaned, pest control, water quality, staff hygiene facilities, and allergen management. Retrofitting a facility that was not designed for it is expensive and sometimes impossible.

Certification and market access

GLOBALG.A.P. or an equivalent farm-level scheme is a common requirement for European retail. It covers food safety, traceability, worker welfare and environmental management at the production level.

GeoGAP — created by the Georgian Farmers' Association with USAID and Chemonics support — is a scaled-down, locally calibrated stepping-stone toward international schemes. It is not a substitute for GLOBALG.A.P. in EU retail, and it is not intended to be. Its function is to make certification achievable for producers who cannot reach an international scheme, building the systems and habits that a later upgrade requires.

I am quoted on this in the Chemonics/USAID technical brief:

"In general, we think that implementation of GeoGAP standards, and going through certification, will give farmers [the] ability to also sell their products at higher prices in the retail sector."

Chemonics / USAID Zrda Activity, A Local Certification System in Georgia, October 2021

Organic certification, where sought, is separate again — its own standard, its own certifying body, its own conversion period, and legal protection on the term itself.

Product specification

Beyond compliance, buyers specify the product: variety, calibre range, kernel shape and colour, moisture content, defect tolerances, packaging and labelling.

Variety and calibre are largely determined at planting. EastFruit reported Guara and Supernova designated for European export at Udabno, with calibre in the 29–30 mm range — which is a market specification driving a planting decision, made once for twenty-five years.

This is the right order. Identifying the target market before ordering trees is what allows the specification to be met; discovering the specification afterwards means matching whatever was planted to whoever will buy it.

Documentation for shipment

Per consignment: commercial invoice and packing list; certificate of origin; phytosanitary certificate where required; analysis certificates including aflatoxin results with sampling documentation; and traceability records linking the consignment to production.

The pattern worth noticing across this whole article: the documentation records compliance that was created upstream. It does not create it.

This site does not claim completed and audited export shipments. Export-oriented production and variety selection for European markets are documented in published sources. Delivered shipments are not.

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: export declarations, phytosanitary certificates, buyer confirmations]

References and further reading

EU requirements described above — maximum residue levels, aflatoxin limits and sampling methodology, general food law traceability obligations, and hygiene requirements — are set out in EU legislation and are amended over time. Verify current limits, approved substances and sampling requirements against the official EU sources for the shipment date rather than relying on any secondary summary, including this one. Certification scheme requirements should be taken from the scheme owners directly.

item.title: Common Deep-Ripping Mistakes, and When Ripping Damages Soil Structure
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Deep ripping has a reputation as an unambiguously good thing to do — a vigorous, obviously beneficial intervention. It is not neutral. It is an expensive, powerful operation that reorganises soil at depth, and on the wrong site or in the wrong conditions it makes things worse permanently.

These are the mistakes I have seen most often, roughly in order of how much they cost.

1. Ripping without confirming a restriction exists

The most common and most expensive. A block is ripped because ripping is what you do before planting, or because a neighbouring block needed it, or because the machine is already on site.

If there is no restriction, ripping achieves nothing and reduces the soil's bearing capacity ahead of harvest traffic.

The fix: dig a pit. See How to Identify a Restrictive Soil Layer.

2. Ripping when the soil is too wet

Covered at length in Correct Soil Moisture for Deep Ripping, and worth repeating because it turns money spent into damage done. Wet soil deforms plastically instead of fracturing: the slot closes, no fracture network forms, and the tine polishes a smeared, low-permeability surface along its whole path.

You have paid to install a new restriction in the shape of your implement.

The fix: the plastic-limit hand test at working depth, and stop-work authority for whoever is watching the soil behind the machine.

3. Blanket specification across variable ground

One pit, or one soil map unit, extended across a whole block or a whole development. Restrictions vary in presence, depth and thickness over short distances. A single specification applied uniformly means some ground is under-treated, some is over-treated, and the cost of the second subsidises the failure of the first.

The fix: enough pits to characterise the variation, and treatment zones that follow it.

4. Bringing unsuitable subsoil into the root zone

The mistake with the worst consequences and the least visibility at the time.

Working deeper than the restriction, on a site where the material below is strongly sodic, saline or acidic, mixes that material upward or opens a pathway for salts to move up into the root zone. On semi-arid sites with saline groundwater, this is a realistic risk rather than a theoretical one.

Sometimes the restrictive layer is doing useful work: perching water and keeping salts away from where roots grow. Fracturing it removes the protection.

The fix: the pit must record what is below the restriction, and where there is any reason to suspect salinity or sodicity — semi-arid climate, saline groundwater, salt crusting anywhere on site, sodic parent material — sample and analyse before specifying any depth.

5. Ripping down the slope

A rip line running downhill is a linear zone of loose, highly permeable soil aligned with water movement. It concentrates flow, accelerates it, and becomes a gully in the shape of the implement path.

On erodible semi-arid soil this can develop within a single significant storm.

The fix: rip across the slope. Where that conflicts with row orientation, the erosion risk takes precedence. See Ripping Depth, Spacing and Direction.

6. Partial penetration

The implement reaches into the restrictive layer but not through it. This is worse than not ripping: the tine tip compacts and smears material at its working depth, creating a new restriction inside the old one, and no connection is made to the permeable material below.

Causes: insufficient drawbar pull, soil too hard, implement not designed for the depth, or a depth specification set by machine capability rather than by the profile.

The fix: know the layer's base depth from the pit, and confirm the machine can reach through it. If it cannot, either get a machine that can, or accept that the site cannot be treated and plan around a shallower rooting volume — which may mean choosing a different crop or a different site.

7. Spacing too wide for the conditions

A spacing set from a specification sheet or previous experience, executed in soil that is fracturing less than expected. Untreated columns remain between passes, and tree positions falling on them get the original restriction and none of the benefit.

The fix: cross-cut trench at the start of the job, measure the actual fracture width, adjust spacing to the soil's behaviour on the day.

8. Ripping after irrigation installation

The sequencing error. Once mainlines and drip lines are in the ground, ripping means destroying the system or leaving untreated strips along the tree rows — the worst possible location for them.

It happens because irrigation and soil preparation are often separate contracts on separate schedules, and irrigation feels urgent as planting approaches.

The fix: whoever manages the programme owns the sequence — assessment, drainage, ripping, settlement, levelling, irrigation, planting — and it is not reorderable.

9. Planting into unsettled ground

Ripped soil is loose and settles: under its own weight, through wetting and drying, and particularly after the first significant rain. Trees planted before settlement sink as the ground drops around them, ending up too deep, sometimes with the graft union buried.

The losses show up years later and get attributed to almost anything else.

The fix: allow a wetting cycle and a settlement period, re-level, then plant. Build it into the establishment timetable rather than treating it as slack.

10. Not checking the work

The specification said 80 cm at 1.5 m spacing. Nobody verified that 80 cm at 1.5 m spacing is what happened, and by the time anything suggests otherwise the trees have been in the ground for three years.

The fix: cross-cut pits during the operation, while the machine is on site and adjustment is still possible. Check depth achieved, lateral fracture continuity, absence of smearing, real fracture rather than slotting.

When deep ripping should not be done at all

Consolidating the cases where the correct decision is not to rip:

No restriction is present. Nothing to gain, bearing capacity to lose.

Soil is too wet, and will not dry within the available window. Wait for next season. Ripping wet is worse than not ripping.

The restriction is beyond machinery reach. Partial penetration worsens conditions. Better to plan around the constraint honestly.

The subsoil is unsuitable. Sodic, saline or strongly acidic material below a restriction is a reason to leave the restriction in place. This needs an analysis, not an impression.

The layer is performing a protective function. A horizon perching water above saline subsoil is protecting the root zone.

Slope and erodibility make it unsafe without erosion control established first.

On a deep sand with no cemented layer. Limited aggregate structure to fracture, limited plasticity, and rapid re-consolidation. Loosening is possible; durable improvement generally is not.

Where the economics favour something else. Ripping is among the most expensive single field operations in establishment. On a marginal site the same capital may achieve considerably more spent on water infrastructure, drainage or erosion control. That comparison should be made explicitly rather than assumed away.

The judgement that took me longest to develop was recognising that the right answer is sometimes "not this block". There is real pressure — commercial, contractual and psychological — to treat land you have committed to. A machine on site and a contractor scheduled generates its own momentum, and "we decided not to" is a harder report to write than "we completed the programme".

But a block that has been assessed and deliberately left alone is a decision. A block that has been ripped wet, or ripped without a restriction, or ripped into saline subsoil, is a liability that cannot be undone.

References and further reading

item.title: Deep Ripping Versus Conventional Subsoiling
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Ask three people in agriculture what the difference is between subsoiling and deep ripping and you will get three answers, at least one of which will be "nothing, it's the same thing with a different name". In casual use that is nearly true. In planning an orchard it is not, because the two operations answer different questions, cost very different amounts, and one of them is a single irreversible opportunity while the other is a recurring maintenance task.

The distinction that matters

Forget depth for a moment. The useful distinction is about what caused the problem you are treating.

Subsoiling treats a restriction created by farming — a compacted layer at or just below the depth of routine cultivation and traffic. Plough pans, tillage pans, and traffic compaction from repeated wheelings all sit in this category. Because the cause is ongoing agricultural activity, the problem re-forms, and the treatment recurs.

Deep ripping treats a deeper restriction that farming did not create — a dense natural horizon, a cemented or indurated layer, long-term consolidation, or a geological discontinuity. The cause is not going to stop, but neither is it going to make the layer re-form once it is fractured. So the treatment is a one-off, and in perennial cropping it is a one-off that has to happen before planting, because afterwards the ground is inaccessible for the life of the orchard.

Why the power difference is not linear

The draught required to pull a tine through soil does not scale in proportion to depth. It rises steeply — a tine working at twice the depth needs considerably more than twice the pull, because it is displacing a larger volume of soil against greater confining pressure, and because deeper material is usually denser and drier.

This has three practical consequences.

Machinery requirements jump rather than climb. A tractor perfectly adequate for subsoiling may be entirely incapable of deep ripping in the same field. This is not a matter of working more slowly; below a certain drawbar pull the implement simply does not reach depth.

Traction matters as much as engine power. Power that cannot be transmitted to the ground is not useful. Weight, ballast, and tyre or track configuration are what convert engine output into pull, which is why tracked or heavily ballasted machines earn their cost in this work.

Cost per hectare rises sharply with specified depth. This is why a quote for ripping is meaningless without a depth and a spacing attached to it. Two quotes at different depths are not comparable, and the cheaper one is often cheaper because it specifies less work.

Deciding which a site needs

The decision is made in a pit, not from a catalogue. Dig, look at the profile face, and answer in order:

1. Is there a restriction at all? No abrupt density change, no platy or massive structure where the surrounding material is crumb or blocky, no roots turning sideways at a consistent depth — then there is nothing to treat, and neither operation is indicated. Loosening soil that is already permeable achieves nothing and reduces its bearing capacity.

2. At what depth is it, and how thick? This is the whole answer to the subsoiling-versus-ripping question. A dense layer at 25–35 cm with looser material above and below is almost certainly cultivation-induced and is a subsoiling problem. A dense layer starting deeper, or one thick enough that its base is well below normal working depth, is a ripping problem.

3. What is below it? This question is skipped more often than any other, and it is the one that turns a good decision into a bad one. If the material beneath the restriction is strongly sodic, saline or otherwise unsuitable, fracturing the layer can bring that material into the root zone or allow salts to move upward. On saline or sodic sites, specifying deep ripping without a salinity assessment is a serious risk. Sometimes the restriction is doing useful work by keeping something worse away from the roots.

4. Can available machinery actually reach and fracture it? Partial penetration is worse than none. A tine that stops within a dense layer without fracturing through it can compact and smear the material at its working depth, creating a new restriction at a new depth.

5. Will the crop use the volume you would gain? For a perennial tree crop with a deep root system in a semi-arid climate, yes, almost always — additional rooting volume is additional stored water. For a shallow-rooted annual, the economics are much less obvious.

The version of this decision I have seen go wrong most often is not choosing the wrong operation. It is specifying either operation across a whole block on the basis of one pit, or on the basis of a soil map, when the restriction is present in part of the block and absent in the rest.

Ripping ground that does not need it is money spent for no return, and it reduces the bearing capacity of soil that will shortly need to carry harvest machinery. Blanket specification is easier to plan and to price. It is also how you pay for treating a problem you did not have.

Where the two operations meet

There is genuine middle ground. Some sites have both a cultivation pan and a deeper restriction, and the sensible answer is a single deeper pass that addresses both, rather than two operations.

There are also implement configurations designed to work at intermediate depths and to fracture laterally with winged or angled tines rather than simply slotting. These blur the categories usefully, and the terminology becomes less important than specifying what you actually want: a fracture network of a given lateral extent, reaching through a layer whose top and bottom depths you have measured.

That specification is unambiguous whatever anyone calls the operation. It is also the only form of specification that can be checked afterwards.

Verifying the work

Whichever operation is done, verify it. Dig a pit across the worked line afterwards and check:

  • Actual depth achieved against specification — measured, not assumed
  • Lateral fracture extending toward the adjacent pass, with no untreated column between them
  • No smeared or polished surfaces on the tine path, which indicate the soil was too wet and the pass has created a new restriction
  • Fracture, not slotting — an open slot with unfractured walls means the operation has achieved almost nothing

Checking a handful of pits across a block while the machine is still on site is the difference between having a specification and having a result.

References and further reading

General principles above are consistent with published guidance on subsoil management from agricultural extension literature — including work on soil compaction diagnosis and amelioration from state and national agricultural research bodies, and standard soil-survey profile description methodology. Where my own field experience is being reported rather than general guidance, it is marked as such above.

item.title: How to Identify a Restrictive Soil Layer
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Almost every expensive mistake in orchard soil preparation traces back to the same omission: nobody confirmed whether a restriction existed, where it was, or how thick it was, before deciding what to do about it.

The confirmation is not difficult. It requires an excavator or a spade, an afternoon, and a willingness to look at what is actually there rather than what the survey data implies. This article is about how to do that and how to read what you find.

Why a soil map is not enough

Soil survey data is genuinely useful. It tells you what soil types occur in an area, what their typical properties are, and roughly where the boundaries fall. It is the right tool for deciding where to investigate.

It is not evidence about a particular block, for straightforward reasons: mapping units are generalisations across areas much larger than a single orchard block; boundaries are interpolated rather than surveyed metre by metre; and compaction and consolidation history — which is often what created the restriction — is not a mapped property at all.

On the land I have worked, the disagreement between mapped expectation and observed profile was frequent enough that we changed how we used the survey entirely. Blocks that mapped as similar behaved differently at depth. Blocks that mapped as poor were sometimes unrestricted below 60 cm. We ended up treating the map as a sampling plan — it told us where to dig — rather than as a finding.

That reframing cost time in the first season and saved considerably more afterwards, because it stopped us specifying uniform treatment across ground that was not uniform.

Digging the pit

Use an excavator if you have one. A machine-dug pit is faster, deeper and gives a cleaner face than hand digging, and depth is the point.

How deep. Deeper than you expect the restriction to be, and deeper than you intend to work. You need to see what is below the layer as well as the layer itself.

How many. More than one, and located to test variation rather than to confirm what you already think. A pit in the best-looking part of the block and a pit in the worst-looking part tell you more than three pits in similar ground. On variable land, plan a pit per management unit rather than per block.

Clean the face. Cut back the smeared surface the bucket leaves. A machine-cut face is polished and hides exactly the structural detail you are looking for. Take a spade or a knife to it until you can see natural structure.

Safety. A pit deep enough to be useful is deep enough to be dangerous. Do not enter an unsupported deep pit. Read the face from outside it, or batter the sides. This is not a formality — soil pit collapses kill people.

Reading the profile face

Work down the face and record what changes and at what depth.

1. Density change you can feel

Push a knife, a screwdriver or a probe horizontally into the face at intervals down the profile. You are feeling for the depth at which resistance increases sharply, and the depth at which it decreases again. Those two numbers — top and bottom of the restriction — are the most important data you will collect, because they determine whether the operation needed is subsoiling or deep ripping, and to what depth.

Resistance that rises and does not fall again within reach is a different and more serious finding: the restriction may be too thick to treat.

2. Structure

Look at how the soil breaks. Above and below a restriction you typically see crumb, granular or blocky structure — aggregates with visible faces, breaking along natural planes.

In the restriction you see one of:

  • Platy structure — horizontal plates, characteristic of compaction. Water and roots move sideways along the plates rather than down through them.
  • Massive structure — no visible aggregation, breaking irregularly. The soil behaves as one coherent lump.
  • Cemented material — genuinely hard, not merely dense, and often needing a hammer rather than a knife.

The distinction matters for treatment. Platy compaction fractures reasonably readily when dry. Strongly cemented material may not fracture usefully at all.

3. Root evidence — the most direct signal available

If anything has been growing on the site, its roots have already run the experiment you are trying to design.

Look for roots that turn horizontally at a consistent depth and run along a boundary rather than crossing it. That is unambiguous evidence of a restriction, at exactly the depth that matters, in this specific soil, under real conditions. No instrument gives you a cleaner answer.

Also look for:

  • Roots flattened or distorted where they have forced through a gap
  • Roots concentrated in cracks and old channels rather than distributed through the matrix — the layer is passable only where something has already made a way
  • No roots at all below a depth, where the soil above is well rooted

4. Colour and mottling

Grey, blue-grey or strongly mottled colours indicate periodic saturation and therefore poor drainage. Immediately above a restriction, that pattern means water is perching on the layer — which tells you the layer restricts water as well as roots, and that drainage may need addressing alongside it.

Orange or rust-coloured mottles and concretions indicate alternating wet and dry conditions.

5. Free water

Standing water in the pit, and the depth at which it appears, is directly informative. Water entering at a specific horizon indicates a perched water table on a restriction. Note it, and note the date and recent rainfall.

6. What is beneath

The question people forget. Record the material below the restriction, and if there is any reason to suspect salinity or sodicity — a semi-arid environment, saline groundwater, salt crusting anywhere on the site, or naturally sodic parent material — sample it and have it analysed before specifying any deep tillage.

Fracturing a layer that separates roots from saline or sodic subsoil can make the site worse. This is the single most consequential thing a pit can tell you, and it is invisible from the surface.

Penetrometer measurements

A cone penetrometer gives resistance against depth as a number, which makes it useful for mapping variation across a block once you know from a pit what you are looking at.

Its limitations need respecting:

  • Readings are strongly moisture-dependent. The same soil reads very differently wet and dry. Comparisons are only meaningful at comparable moisture, which in practice means surveying within a short period.
  • Stones give false high readings. A stone at 40 cm reads like a pan at 40 cm.
  • It tells you resistance, not cause. It cannot distinguish platy compaction from cemented material from a stone layer — and those need different responses.

Used properly the sequence is: pit first to establish what the profile is and what the restriction consists of; penetrometer afterwards to map how that restriction varies across the area, at consistent moisture.

Reversing the order produces numbers without meaning.

Bulk density

Bulk-density sampling — a known volume, dried and weighed — gives the most quantitative measure of compaction, and is worth doing where a decision is genuinely marginal or where you want a baseline to measure improvement against later.

It is slow, needs care to sample the right horizon without disturbing it, and requires interpretation against the soil's texture, since the density at which roots are restricted differs substantially between a sand and a clay. It is a confirmation tool rather than a survey tool.

Recording it properly

Whatever you find is worth recording in a form that will still make sense in three years, when someone asks why a block was treated the way it was:

  • Location — GPS coordinate, not "the pit near the gate"
  • Date, and recent rainfall
  • Depth of every horizon boundary
  • Structure, colour and density for each horizon
  • Root observations, especially the depth of lateral deflection
  • Free water depth if present
  • A photograph of the clean face with a tape measure in frame
  • Samples taken and analyses requested

The photograph requirement is not optional. A soil profile photograph without a scale in it cannot support a statement about depth — which is the main thing it would be needed for.

References and further reading

The profile-description method above follows standard soil-survey practice as set out in national soil description handbooks and field guides. Guidance on compaction diagnosis, penetrometer limitations and bulk-density interpretation is consistent with published agricultural extension material on soil physical constraints. Field observations flagged above are my own.

item.title: Irrigation Planning for Almond Orchards
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Almond orchards in semi-arid conditions are entirely irrigation-dependent, which means the irrigation system does not support the yield ceiling — it is the yield ceiling. A design decision made once, before planting, constrains the orchard for twenty-five years.

Most of the serious mistakes are made in sizing and in uniformity, not in equipment selection.

Size to peak demand, not average

The most consequential design error, and the most common.

Almond water demand is strongly seasonal. It rises through spring, peaks during the kernel-fill period in mid to late summer, and falls after harvest. The peak is substantially higher than the annual average.

A system sized to average annual demand will be unable to meet the peak. That shortfall arrives during kernel fill — the period when water deficit most directly reduces yield and kernel quality. So the system fails at precisely the moment failure is most expensive, every year, permanently.

Sizing to peak requires:

  • Peak crop evapotranspiration for a mature orchard at full canopy — not for the young trees being planted now. The system has to serve the orchard it will become.
  • Application efficiency factored in — the system delivers less to the root zone than it discharges.
  • Leaching requirement added where water quality demands it (below).
  • Realistic operating hours. A system that can meet peak demand only by running 24 hours a day has no capacity for maintenance, no recovery from a breakdown, and no margin in an exceptional season.

That last point is a recurring trap. On paper the system meets peak demand; in practice it can only do so at 100% utilisation, so any failure becomes an immediate crop-loss event.

Distribution uniformity

The metric that matters most and is monitored least.

A system delivering the correct average volume with poor uniformity over-waters part of the block and under-waters the rest. This is worse than uniformly slightly inadequate irrigation:

  • The under-watered fraction loses yield, and accumulates salt because there is insufficient water to leach it
  • The over-watered fraction loses yield through waterlogging and root disease, wastes water, and leaches nutrients below the root zone
  • The block becomes unmanageable as a unit — no single scheduling decision is correct for all of it, permanently

Uniformity is a design property that degrades in service through emitter blockage, wear, and pressure variation across topography. And the degradation is invisible from a vehicle: the trees look similar for a year or two before the divergence becomes obvious, by which point it is embedded in the canopy.

What it requires:

  • Pressure regulation across elevation change. On sloping ground, unregulated systems deliver very different volumes at different heights.
  • Correct lateral lengths so pressure loss along a line stays within the emitter's compensating range.
  • Pressure-compensating emitters where topography justifies them.
  • Measurement, not assumption. Periodic flow checks at emitters distributed across the block — beginning, middle and end of laterals, top and bottom of slopes.

Filtration

Blocked emitters are the primary cause of uniformity loss, and filtration is what prevents them.

Match filtration to the water source: surface water carries organic material and algae; groundwater carries sand and can carry dissolved iron and manganese that precipitate in the lines; recycled or stored water can carry biological growth.

Design points:

  • Filtration finer than the emitter's susceptibility threshold
  • Automatic backflush on a large system — manual cleaning does not happen reliably at scale
  • Pressure differential monitoring across the filter to indicate fouling
  • Chemical treatment capability for biological growth and mineral precipitation
  • Flushing valves at lateral ends, and a flushing regime that is actually carried out

Under-specifying filtration is a false economy that shows up as permanent uniformity loss.

Scheduling

Irrigate against measured demand and measured soil status, not against a calendar.

Crop demand estimated from reference evapotranspiration and a crop coefficient appropriate to canopy development and growth stage.

Soil moisture monitored at more than one depth — typically within the main root zone and below it. Two depths tell you something one cannot: whether you are refilling the root zone or pushing water past it.

Growth stage sensitivity. Almonds are most sensitive to water deficit during kernel fill. Some regions practise controlled deficit irrigation at specific lower-sensitivity stages, which is a legitimate technique but requires confident monitoring — it is deficit by design, and indistinguishable from deficit by accident if you are not measuring.

Post-harvest irrigation matters for the following season's bud development, and is the irrigation most often neglected because the crop is already off.

Fertigation

Applying nutrients through the irrigation system is standard practice in drip-irrigated orchards, and the reasoning is straightforward: with drip irrigation, the active root zone is concentrated in the wetted volume, so nutrients placed there are available and nutrients broadcast outside it largely are not.

Requirements: injection equipment with accurate metering; backflow prevention (non-negotiable, and often a legal requirement); compatibility checking between fertiliser products and water chemistry to avoid precipitation in the lines; and a flushing regime after each injection.

The benefit is precision — small, frequent applications matched to demand through the season, rather than large infrequent applications that leach.

Leaching requirement

In semi-arid irrigated agriculture, every irrigation adds salt and there is not enough rainfall to remove it. Unless a deliberate excess is applied to move salts below the root zone, they accumulate.

Which means the leaching requirement is part of the water budget, calculated from irrigation water salinity and the crop's salinity tolerance — and almonds are relatively salt-sensitive, so the requirement is meaningful.

Two things have to be true for leaching to work:

  1. Water is applied in excess of crop demand by the leaching fraction
  2. Drainage exists to carry the leached water away

Leaching without drainage does not remove the problem; it moves salt down to a water table that then rises. This is why drainage assessment precedes irrigation design rather than following it.

Interaction with soil preparation

Two hard sequencing rules, both consequences of the same fact — that you cannot get under an orchard once it exists:

Deep ripping precedes irrigation installation. Always. Installing mainlines and laterals first means either destroying them to rip, or leaving untreated strips along the tree rows. See Ripping Depth, Spacing and Direction.

Drainage precedes ripping. Fracturing soil into a site with an unresolved water table produces a fissure network that fills with water.

And a design consequence: soil preparation changes the soil's water-holding and infiltration behaviour, so irrigation design should be based on the soil's post-ripping properties, not on the pre-treatment assessment.

Young orchard versus mature orchard

The system must serve a mature orchard but will first operate on newly planted trees with tiny root systems and minimal canopy.

  • Emitter layout for a young tree may need to differ from the mature layout, or the emitters near each tree need to be usable independently
  • Young trees need frequent, small applications — their root volume holds almost no water
  • Applying mature-orchard volumes to young trees wastes water, leaches nutrients, and can waterlog and kill the trees you have just planted
  • Design for staged operation so the system can be run appropriately at each phase

Maintenance as a design requirement

A drip system is a maintenance commitment for the orchard's life, and designing without planning for that produces a system that performs well for three years and poorly for twenty-two.

Build in: filter backflush and monitoring; lateral flushing valves and a flushing schedule; emitter flow checking as a routine, recorded activity; pressure monitoring at fixed points; and leak detection.

Uniformity monitoring is the maintenance activity that gets dropped first and costs most. It produces no visible result on the day it is done, unlike fixing a leak, and it requires walking the block with a measuring container rather than driving past it.

The consequence appears two or three years later as blocks that are permanently uneven — trees of different sizes in the same planting, needing different management that they cannot receive because they share an irrigation zone. By then it is a structural feature of the orchard, not a maintenance backlog.

item.title: Machinery Requirements for Large Almond Operations
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Machinery planning for a large almond operation is usually approached as a procurement exercise: what do we need, and what does it cost. That framing produces fleets that are simultaneously over-invested and incapable, because it does not address the two questions that actually determine outcomes — what the chain's constraint is, and whether the machinery can do the soil work the site requires.

The harvest chain and its constraint

Mechanical almond harvest is a sequence:

  1. Shaking — trunk or canopy shakers remove nuts from the tree
  2. Drying on the orchard floor (in systems that use floor drying) or direct catching
  3. Sweeping — nuts windrowed from the floor
  4. Pick-up — the windrow collected
  5. Transport — to the processing facility
  6. Receiving, hulling and drying at the facility

The chain runs at the speed of its slowest element. This sounds obvious and is routinely ignored in fleet planning.

If receiving and drying capacity at the facility is the constraint, an additional shaker adds nothing. It moves nuts off trees faster into a queue that is already full, and product waiting in the field or in trailers is product losing quality and accumulating aflatoxin risk.

So fleet sizing is calculated backward:

processing receiving and drying throughput
   → tonnes per day the facility can absorb
      → transport capacity to deliver that rate
         → pick-up capacity to supply the transport
            → sweeping capacity to supply the pick-up
               → shaking capacity to supply the sweeping

Any element sized above the facility's throughput is capital purchased to create a queue. Any element below it under-uses the facility, which is usually the most expensive asset in the chain.

See Almond Processing and Export Development.

Harvest window length

Capacity requirement is total crop divided by available window. So the window's length is a fleet-sizing input, and it is determined by:

  • Variety maturity spread. Multiple varieties maturing at different times spread the load. A single variety across a large area concentrates the entire crop into one narrow window — which is a capacity problem created at planting, years before anyone specifies machinery.
  • Weather risk. Rain during harvest stops floor operations and raises quality risk. The window has to include contingency for days lost.
  • Quality deterioration. Nuts left too long on the tree or on the ground lose quality.

This is why variety selection is a machinery decision as much as a market one. See Almond Orchard Development.

Tractors and soil work

The mechanization requirement that determines what the site can become, rather than just how efficiently it operates.

Deep tillage needs drawbar pull, not engine power. Pull requires weight, appropriate ballast, and tyre or track configuration adequate to transmit it. Engine power that cannot reach the ground is not useful. On heavy, dry, compacted soil, if the available pull cannot bring a ripper through the restrictive layer at the required depth, that layer stays — permanently, because the ground is inaccessible after planting.

Manufacturer figures are optimistic for these conditions. Draught requirements in dry, hard, stony ground are substantially higher than in the conditions used for specification, and progress rates correspondingly lower. Plan on observed rates from comparable ground, not on brochure figures.

Weight is a liability outside the job it is required for. The same mass that provides traction for ripping causes compaction in every other operation. A fleet built entirely around the heaviest task compacts the soil it was bought to improve.

The resolution is segregation — by machine, by traffic lane, and by timing:

  • Heavy machines reserved for the operations that need them
  • Lighter machines for routine spraying, mowing and orchard management
  • Traffic confined to permanent lanes, which in an orchard is largely automatic once rows are established — making the alignment decisions at establishment more consequential than they look
  • Avoiding traffic on wet soil, which is an operational discipline rather than an investment

See Agricultural Mechanization and Deep-Ripping and Soil Preparation.

Implement matching

The implement does the work.

  • Ripper configuration — shank number, spacing and geometry matched to the target depth and the soil's fracture behaviour, which is observed rather than assumed. See Ripping Depth, Spacing and Direction.
  • Wear parts as a consumable with a performance effect. In stony ground, wear is a major operating cost — and a worn shank changes the geometry of the work. A blunt point smears where a sharp one fractures. Wear affects results, not only budget.
  • Depth control hardware — consistency matters more than maximum depth.
  • Sprayers matched to canopy volume and to residue compliance requirements, since application accuracy determines whether the crop meets EU maximum residue levels.
  • Mowers and floor management equipment, since orchard floor condition determines harvest efficiency and product cleanliness.

Orchard floor — a machinery decision made at establishment

Mechanical harvest picks nuts off the ground, so the ground's condition determines harvest efficiency and product cleanliness.

Requirements: level and smooth enough for sweepers and pick-up machines to operate close to the surface without picking up soil; free of surface stones, which enter the product and wear processing equipment; firm enough to carry harvest traffic; and shaped so water does not pond.

All of this is decided at establishment — levelling after ripping and settlement, stone removal, surface shaping. It cannot be meaningfully improved once trees are in the ground, and it costs harvest efficiency and product quality every season for twenty-five years.

Maintenance capability

On a large operation, maintenance capability is part of the machinery decision, not a consequence of it.

  • Workshop capacity proportionate to the fleet, with the skills to do more than routine servicing
  • Critical spares held on site for harvest-window failures. A delay during harvest is not recoverable within the season, and a part on a two-week lead time is a crop-loss event.
  • Scheduled maintenance timed against the operational calendar so it happens before the window, not during it
  • Operator training. The same machine in different hands produces measurably different work, and in deep tillage the difference is large.
  • Records — hours, failures, costs — so replacement decisions are made on data

Serviceability in the actual location

In a market without an established machinery base, this frequently outranks performance specification.

A machine that cannot be repaired locally within the harvest window is a risk regardless of how good it is. Assess: parts availability and realistic lead times; dealer technical support and its response time; whether local technicians have the skills and diagnostic equipment; and how many similar machines exist in the country, because a machine with no local population has no informal support network and no second-hand parts.

Operator skill is consistently underweighted in mechanization planning, and in deep tillage it is decisive. The operator controls depth consistency and ground speed, and makes the judgement about whether conditions are suitable at all — which is the judgement that determines whether a pass fractures the soil or smears it.

Training operators to read the soil behind the machine, and explicitly giving them authority to stop when it looked wrong, improved our outcomes more than any individual equipment decision. It also cost nothing.

References and further reading

item.title: Reducing Erosion in Semi-Arid Agricultural Land
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
On semi-arid agricultural land, erosion is the fastest way to lose the asset itself. Yield can recover from a bad season; soil that has left the site does not come back.

Two mechanisms operate, and they need different responses. Water erosion arrives in short intense storms falling on ground that infiltrates poorly, and it does most of its damage in a small number of events. Wind erosion works on dry, bare, fine-textured soil with weak aggregate stability, and it operates continuously whenever those conditions coincide with wind.

Layout is the primary control

The most effective erosion control on a perennial planting is decided at establishment, in the layout, and is nearly impossible to retrofit afterwards.

Align across the slope, not down it

Rows, traffic lanes and — critically — rip lines should run across the slope rather than down it.

A rip line running downhill is a drain. It is a linear zone of loosened, highly permeable soil aligned with the direction of water movement. Water concentrates in it, accelerates, carries soil, and the channel deepens. On erodible semi-arid soil this can develop within a single significant storm, producing a gully in the exact shape of the implement path.

Where alignment across the slope conflicts with the preferred row orientation, the erosion risk takes precedence. Untreated soil columns between ripping passes cost yield in some tree positions; a gully system costs the soil, and it does not stop once it has started.

See Ripping Depth, Spacing and Direction.

Design roads as part of the drainage system

Roads and tracks concentrate water by definition — they are compacted, often slightly sunken, and impermeable relative to their surroundings. A road network designed without reference to water movement becomes the site's drainage network by default, and an uncontrolled one.

Design in: cross-fall and cross-drains at intervals; discharge points that release water onto stable ground or into a designed waterway rather than onto erodible soil; and alignment that avoids running long distances directly downslope.

Place windbreaks in the layout

Windbreaks are far more effective when planned as part of block layout than added later. Retrofitting means finding space between established rows, and losing production area to trees that take years to become effective.

Ground cover, and the water trade-off

Cover is the single most effective protection against both mechanisms. In semi-arid conditions it also competes for the resource that limits the crop, which makes it a genuine trade-off rather than an obvious good.

The hierarchy, best to worst:

  1. Living permanent cover in the inter-row — protects the surface, adds organic matter, improves aggregate stability and infiltration
  2. Residue or mulch — protects the surface without transpiring water
  3. Bare soil — no protection

The competition is real: a living cover crop transpires water the orchard needs, and in a water-limited system that can directly reduce yield. The decision depends on species choice, termination timing, the season's rainfall, and how much water is genuinely available.

Where water does not allow living cover, residue is the fallback and it is substantially better than nothing. Where neither is possible, the operational discipline below carries more weight.

See Regenerative Agriculture in Semi-Arid Georgia.

Treat the concentration points

The observation that changes how erosion control is budgeted: most erosion originates at a small number of identifiable places.

Not uniformly across fields — at:

  • Road edges and culvert outlets
  • Headlands and turning areas
  • Block corners, where water from two directions converges
  • Natural drainage lines crossing worked ground
  • Points where a rip line or wheel track intersects a slope
  • Discharge points from any drainage structure

These points are a small fraction of the area and produce a large fraction of the damage. Treating them — armouring, energy dissipation, stable grassed waterways, reshaping to spread rather than concentrate flow — is far cheaper and more effective than any whole-field treatment.

The practical method that worked was walking the site immediately after the first significant storm of the season, before anything was repaired, and photographing every place water had visibly concentrated or moved soil.

That walk identifies the real problem points, which are consistently fewer and more specific than a desk assessment predicts, and sometimes in places nobody expected. Fixing them individually over the following dry season addressed most of the site's erosion at a fraction of what a general treatment programme would have cost.

Repeating the walk each year shows whether the fixes held and where new problems have appeared as the site changed.

Wind erosion

Distinct from water erosion and often underestimated on land that is dry most of the year.

Conditions that produce it: dry surface soil, fine texture, weak aggregate stability, no cover, and wind. On a semi-arid site in summer, four of those five are permanent features.

Controls:

  • Do not cultivate dry, bare soil in windy conditions. This is an operational rule requiring no capital, and it is the single most effective wind-erosion control available.
  • Maintain surface roughness. A rough surface traps moving particles; a fine, smooth, well-worked surface is the most erodible condition you can create.
  • Retain residue wherever possible.
  • Windbreaks to reduce wind speed at the surface.
  • Avoid excessive secondary cultivation. Each pass breaks aggregates down further, producing exactly the fine, loose material that moves.

The last point deserves emphasis because it runs against a common instinct. A finely worked, level, tidy-looking seedbed is the most erodible surface achievable. Tidiness and erosion resistance are opposed.

Improving the soil's own resistance

Beyond protecting the surface, the soil can be made less erodible.

Aggregate stability determines whether aggregates survive raindrop impact and wetting. It is closely tied to organic matter and to biological activity, is cheap and quick to test, and is a better indicator of erosion risk than most alternatives.

Infiltration rate determines how much rainfall enters rather than running off. Improving it addresses water erosion at source — water that infiltrates does not erode. Compaction reduces it, which is one reason compaction management is erosion management.

Organic matter underpins both, and in semi-arid conditions accumulates slowly and is lost quickly. Gains built over a decade can be lost in one badly timed cultivation.

Sodicity is worth checking specifically. Sodic soils disperse on wetting — clay particles separate rather than staying aggregated — which makes them highly erodible and seals the surface against infiltration, producing runoff. If a site erodes more than its texture and slope suggest it should, sodicity is a likely explanation, and gypsum amelioration addresses the cause rather than the symptom.

See Soil Requirements for Commercial Almond Orchards.

Monitoring

Erosion is gradual and easy not to notice until it is severe. What makes it visible:

  • Fixed photo points — same locations, same framing, annually. This is the cheapest monitoring available and the most convincing evidence of change in either direction.
  • The post-storm walk, photographed and recorded.
  • Measuring soil depth at marked points over years.
  • Recording sediment accumulation in drains, dams and low points — what accumulates there left somewhere else.
  • Watching for exposure of subsoil or stone at the surface in patches, which indicates the topsoil above has gone.

References and further reading

Erosion mechanisms and control measures above are consistent with standard soil-conservation guidance — contour alignment, cover management, concentration-point treatment, wind-erosion control through surface roughness and residue retention, and sodicity's role in dispersion and surface sealing. Field methods flagged as personal practice are my own.

item.title: Ripping Depth, Spacing and Direction
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Once you have established that a restriction exists and that the soil is dry enough to treat it, three parameters remain: how deep, how far apart, and in which direction. Each has a plausible-sounding wrong answer.

Depth

The rule: deep enough to penetrate and fracture through the restriction, and no deeper.

The depth is a property of the soil profile, not of the machine. Your pit gave you the top and bottom of the restrictive layer; the target is to work through the base of it and slightly beyond, so that fractures connect the material above the layer with the permeable material below.

Why deeper is not better

Draught rises steeply with depth. Not proportionally — considerably faster. Each additional increment of depth costs disproportionately more in fuel, time and wear, and may exceed the machine's capability entirely.

Depth beyond the restriction buys nothing. If the layer bottoms out at 70 cm and the material below is permeable and root-friendly, working at 110 cm treats soil that did not need treating.

It can make things worse. Working below the restriction may bring up unsuitable material — sodic, saline or acidic subsoil — into the profile. This is the most serious reason for restraint, and it is why the pit needs to record what lies below the layer, not just where the layer is.

Loosened soil has reduced bearing capacity. Deeper loosening means a deeper weakened zone, which then has to carry harvest machinery.

Consistency beats maximum

Uniform depth across the block matters more than peak depth in the best spots. Variable depth leaves untreated sections, and trees planted above them perform differently from their neighbours for the orchard's life — producing a block that looks patchy and is difficult to manage as a unit.

This makes depth control a real specification item: implement geometry, depth wheels or skids, operator attention, and ground-speed consistency.

Project-specific working depths from orchards I have worked on are not published here, pending documentation. [VERIFICATION REQUIRED: dated work records, soil profile descriptions, machinery specifications]

The method for determining the correct depth on any given site — measure the layer in a pit and work through its base — does not depend on those figures.

Spacing

The rule: close enough that fracture zones from adjacent passes intersect, leaving no untreated column between them.

That is a statement about the soil's fracture behaviour, which you have to observe rather than assume, because it varies with moisture, texture, structure and depth.

Determining it empirically

The reliable method takes one pit:

  1. Make two passes at a trial spacing
  2. Excavate a trench perpendicular to both passes
  3. Look at the cross-section: how far does visible fracturing extend sideways from each tine path, and do the two zones meet?

If they meet with overlap, the spacing is adequate or could be widened slightly. If there is intact, unfractured soil between them, close the spacing.

Doing this at the start of the job, on the actual soil, at the actual moisture, answers the question definitively. Every alternative is inference.

What changes the answer

  • Moisture. Drier, more brittle soil fractures further. See Correct Soil Moisture for Deep Ripping. Spacing and moisture cannot be decided independently.
  • Depth. Fracture is generally narrower at greater depth, under higher confining pressure. A spacing that gives continuous fracture at 50 cm may leave untreated columns at 90 cm.
  • Texture and structure. Well-aggregated soils propagate cracks along existing planes of weakness. Massive or cemented material fractures less predictably.
  • Tine geometry. Winged or angled tines fracture wider than plain narrow shanks and allow wider spacing at the cost of higher draught.

The consequence of getting it wrong

An untreated column between passes is not a minor imperfection. If tree positions happen to fall on those columns — and with a regular planting grid over a regular ripping pattern, some of them will — those trees have the original restriction beneath them and none of the benefit that was paid for.

This is why row alignment and ripping pattern have to be planned together rather than sequentially.

Direction

Two considerations, which frequently conflict.

Consideration 1: orchard row alignment

Tree positions should sit in treated ground. The two workable approaches:

Rip along the future row lines. Simple, ensures every tree sits on a ripped line, and economical because you are not treating the inter-row to the same standard. The limitation is that rooting volume is developed along the row and less across it.

Rip in a grid, or at an angle to the rows. More passes and more cost, but develops rooting volume in two directions and removes the risk of a tree position falling between passes.

Which is right depends on how confident you are in the eventual row positions. If the layout is fixed, along-the-row ripping is efficient. If layout may change — and on a large development it often does — a grid or angled pattern is insurance, and the extra cost buys the removal of a permanent risk.

Consideration 2: slope and water — and this one wins

A rip line running down a slope is a drain. It is a linear zone of loosened, highly permeable soil oriented along the direction of water movement. On erodible semi-arid soil, that is the beginning of a gully, and it will be a gully in the shape of your implement path.

Water concentrates in it, moves fast, carries soil, and the channel deepens. What was intended to improve infiltration becomes the site's primary erosion pathway.

So on sloping ground, rip across the slope. On contour, or as close to it as the machinery can safely and practically work.

Where this conflicts with row orientation, the erosion risk takes precedence. Untreated columns cost yield in some tree positions. A gully system costs the soil itself, and it does not stop once started.

Where row orientation is genuinely fixed and conflicts with the contour, the answer is to rip across the slope anyway and manage the row-alignment issue through spacing — a tighter pattern so that every row position falls within a fracture zone regardless of orientation.

Sequencing with drainage and irrigation

Order matters, and one step in particular is not negotiable.

  1. Assessment — pits, profiles, drainage evaluation, salinity checks
  2. Drainage installation, if required. Before ripping: fracturing soil into a site with an unresolved water table produces a fissure network that fills with water and concentrates it with nowhere to go
  3. Deep ripping — correct moisture, depth, spacing, direction
  4. Settlement period — a wetting cycle, ideally natural rainfall
  5. Surface levelling and shaping — after settlement, so the finished surface is the settled surface
  6. Irrigation installation
  7. Planting

Step 6 is where the expensive mistake happens

Deep ripping must precede irrigation installation. If drip lines, mainlines and sub-mains are in the ground first, ripping means either destroying them or leaving untreated strips exactly along the tree rows — which is the worst possible place for them.

It happens because irrigation installation is often on a different contract and a different schedule from soil preparation, and because irrigation feels like the urgent item when planting is approaching. Whoever is managing the programme has to own this sequence explicitly.

And step 4 is not slack in the schedule

Ripped ground settles — under its own weight, through wetting and drying, and notably after the first significant rainfall. Planting into unsettled ground means trees sink as the soil drops around them, ending up too deep, with stem or graft union burial. The losses from that appear years later and are attributed to everything except the planting depth.

Allow a wetting cycle and a settlement period, then re-level, then plant.

Verifying the work

The specification is worth nothing unless the result is checked. Dig a pit across the rip lines after the operation and confirm:

  • Depth achieved, measured, against specification
  • Lateral fracture meeting between adjacent passes, with no intact column
  • No smearing or polishing on tine paths
  • Genuine fracture rather than slotting — an open slot with intact walls means the pass achieved very little
  • No unsuitable subsoil material brought into the upper profile

A few pits across a block, while the machine is still on site and adjustments are still possible, is what turns a plan into an outcome.

References and further reading

Guidance on draught–depth relationships, fracture behaviour and tine geometry above is consistent with published soil-tillage engineering literature and agricultural extension material on subsoiling practice. Recommendations on contour orientation and erosion risk follow standard soil-conservation practice for sloping land. Sequencing recommendations reflect my own project experience, marked where relevant.

item.title: Correct Soil Moisture for Deep Ripping
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
If you take one thing from everything written here about deep ripping, take this: soil moisture at the time of the operation matters more than depth, spacing, machine power or operator skill. Everything else can be adequate and the pass will still fail if the soil is too wet. And the failure is not neutral — you will have spent the money and created a new problem.

Two failure modes

Soil under a moving tine does one of two things, and which one depends almost entirely on water content.

Brittle failure — what you want

Dry soil is brittle. Aggregates are held by cohesive forces that, once exceeded, break rather than yield. When a tine passes through, stress propagates ahead and outward, and the soil fractures: cracks radiate from the tine path, upward and sideways, well beyond the physical width of the implement.

The result is a network of interconnected fissures. Roots exploit them, water infiltrates through them, air exchanges through them. The treated volume is much larger than the volume the tine displaced, which is the whole economic basis of the operation — you are paying for a fracture network, not for a slot.

Plastic failure — what you get if you rip wet

Wet soil is plastic. Water lubricates the particle surfaces, aggregates deform instead of breaking, and the soil flows around the tine and closes behind it.

Three things happen, all bad:

  1. No fracture network. Stress does not propagate; it is absorbed in local deformation. You get a slot the width of the tine and nothing beyond it.
  2. The slot closes. Plastic soil flows back. Within a season the slot may be largely undetectable.
  3. The tine polishes the soil it passes through. The sliding surface smears and seals, producing a dense, low-permeability skin along the entire tine path.

That third effect is the serious one. You have created a new restrictive surface, at depth, in the shape of your implement path — often less permeable than the layer you were trying to remove. This is why ripping wet is worse than not ripping at all.

Judging the window in the field

The target is soil that is dry, throughout the depth you intend to work. Not dry at the surface — dry at depth, which is a different question and needs checking at depth.

The hand test

Crude, immediate, and reliable enough to make the decision. Take soil from the target depth — from a pit or a deep auger sample, not from the surface — and:

Try to roll a thread. Roll a portion between your palms into a thread a few millimetres thick.

  • It will not form; it crumbles → soil is at or below the plastic limit. This is the condition you want.
  • It rolls into a coherent thread that bends without breaking → soil is plastic. Do not rip.
  • It rolls easily and feels slick, marks your hands → far too wet. Do not cultivate at all.

Squeeze a handful. If it holds together as a cast and glistens, it is too wet. If it crumbles under light pressure into aggregates, it is workable.

This is the classic plastic-limit field test, and it is the same test used for deciding whether to travel on soil at all. It takes a minute and it answers the question.

Check at depth, and at more than one place

Surface moisture is a poor guide to moisture at 80 cm. The profile can be dust-dry on top and plastic below, particularly early in the dry season or above a perched water table. Auger or dig at the working depth.

Do this at several locations across the block. Low-lying areas, shaded areas and areas above a restriction all dry more slowly, and a block is often ready in one part and not in another.

Behind the machine — the check that matters most

The most reliable indicator is the soil's behaviour during the pass. Watch behind the implement:

  • Good conditions: visible heave and cracking, soil breaking into clods, a fracture pattern extending sideways from the tine line
  • Marginal conditions: heave without much lateral cracking, larger cohesive clods
  • Bad conditions: a clean slot with smooth walls, soil closing behind the tine, a shiny surface on the slot walls

That last picture means stop. Not "carry on more slowly" — stop, and come back when the soil is drier.

Making this a stop-work authority for operators rather than a management decision changed our outcomes more than any equipment change.

The pressure to continue is always considerable. The machine is on site, the contractor is scheduled, the planting programme is fixed, and the difference between acceptable and unacceptable conditions is not obvious from a vehicle window. If the only person who can stop the job is not the person watching the soil, the job does not get stopped.

Training operators to read the soil behind the machine, and making it explicit that stopping was the correct decision and would not be held against them, was the whole intervention.

Why the window is inconveniently narrow

The conditions that make ripping effective are also the conditions that make it difficult and expensive:

  • Dry soil is hard, so draught is high and progress is slow
  • Wear on shanks and points is much higher in dry, hard ground
  • The dry window may be short, and every contractor wants it at the same time
  • In an irrigated system, the dry window may have to be created by withholding water — which is only possible before planting

None of that changes the physics. A site that is not dry enough should wait, and where waiting means deferring planting by a season, that is usually the cheaper option compared with a failed pass plus a new engineered restriction.

Interaction with spacing

Moisture and spacing are a single coupled decision, not two independent ones.

Fracture propagates further laterally in drier, more brittle soil. So:

  • Drier soil → wider fracture → wider spacing acceptable
  • Moister soil → narrower fracture → spacing must be closer to achieve continuity

Which means a spacing specified for dry conditions, executed in moister conditions, leaves untreated columns between passes — with the trees very possibly planted into them. The specification and the conditions have to be reconciled on the day, not in the office weeks earlier.

The practical answer is to check the achieved fracture width in a cross-cut pit at the start of the job, and adjust spacing to what the soil is actually doing.

See Ripping Depth, Spacing and Direction.

Timing in the season

In a semi-arid climate with winter-dominant rainfall, the profile is normally driest in late summer to early autumn. That is the natural window.

Planning implications:

  • Programme ripping for the end of the dry season, before autumn rain
  • Allow time after ripping for a wetting and settlement cycle before planting — ideally natural rainfall
  • Do not compress the sequence to fit a planting date. Ripping into damp soil to meet a nursery delivery is a poor trade: the trees arrive on time into soil that has not been improved and may have been damaged

Where irrigation exists and the site is pre-planting, withholding water to dry the profile deliberately is a legitimate tactic — it is the one opportunity to control the variable rather than wait for it.

The exception worth knowing

Very sandy soils with little clay behave differently. They have limited plasticity at any realistic water content and limited cohesion, so they neither fracture in a sustained network nor smear appreciably. Loosening them is possible; producing a durable fracture network is not, because there is little aggregate structure to fracture.

Sandy soils also re-consolidate faster. Whether ripping is worth doing at all on a deep sand depends on whether the restriction is a genuine cemented or compacted layer — which does occur in sands — or simply density, which will return.

References and further reading

The brittle/plastic failure distinction and the plastic-limit field test are standard soil-mechanics and soil-management material, described in agricultural extension guidance on tillage timing and in soil-physics texts. Recommendations on seasonal timing and the moisture–spacing interaction are consistent with published subsoiling guidance. Field practice reported above is my own.
