item.title: Soil Requirements for Commercial Almond Orchards
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Almonds are commercially attractive and agronomically demanding. They are also unusually unforgiving about soil, in two specific ways that between them account for most orchard failures: they will not tolerate waterlogging, and in a dry climate they depend heavily on a deep rooting volume to buffer between irrigations.

Both are properties you establish before planting or accept for twenty-five years.

Depth — the property that sets the ceiling

An almond tree's water supply is the water held in the soil its roots can occupy. In an irrigated semi-arid system, that stored volume is the buffer between one irrigation and the next, and the buffer against any interruption in supply.

A shallow rooting volume means:

  • No tolerance for irrigation interruption. A pump failure or a supply restriction during nut fill becomes a stress event within days rather than weeks.
  • Higher irrigation frequency, and therefore higher operating cost and greater system dependence.
  • Reduced total water availability at peak demand, which caps yield regardless of nutrition or canopy management.
  • Greater salinity risk, because a small soil volume subject to frequent irrigation concentrates salts faster.

The practical requirement is a deep, unrestricted profile. Where a restriction exists within the rooting zone, the decision is whether it can be removed before planting — see Deep-Ripping and Soil Preparation — because it cannot be removed afterwards.

How to assess it: a pit, not a map. Record the depth of any density change, structural discontinuity or root-limiting horizon, and what lies below it. See How to Identify a Restrictive Soil Layer.

Drainage — the property that kills trees

Almonds are markedly intolerant of waterlogging. Saturated soil excludes oxygen from the root zone, and roots that are anaerobic for even short periods are damaged and become susceptible to root and crown diseases — Phytophthora being the recurring problem in orchards on poorly drained ground.

The awkward part is that this applies on land that is dry most of the year. Semi-arid sites can have serious drainage problems:

  • Intense storm rainfall on soil that infiltrates poorly, ponding on the surface
  • Perched water tables on a restrictive layer, saturating the profile above it after irrigation or rain
  • Rising water tables induced by irrigation itself over a period of years
  • Low-lying positions and depressions that receive run-on from surrounding ground

How to assess it: the pit again. Grey, blue-grey or strongly mottled colours indicate periodic saturation. Free water in the pit, and the depth at which it appears, indicates a water table or perching. Orange mottles and concretions indicate alternating wet and dry conditions.

Assess drainage before designing irrigation, and install drainage before deep ripping where both are needed — ripping into a site with an unresolved water table produces a fissure network that fills and concentrates water with nowhere to go.

Texture and structure

Almonds do best on medium-textured soils — loams and sandy loams — that combine adequate water-holding capacity with free drainage and good aeration.

Sands drain freely and aerate well but hold little water, requiring frequent irrigation and offering minimal buffer. Workable with high-frequency drip, but unforgiving of system failure.

Heavy clays hold water well but drain slowly, aerate poorly, and are prone to both waterlogging and compaction. They are also the soils most likely to have a restrictive layer and the hardest to treat, because they smear readily when moist.

Structure matters as much as texture. A well-aggregated clay loam can perform far better than its texture suggests, while a structurally degraded loam can behave like a much heavier soil. What you are looking for in the pit is visible aggregation — crumb or blocky structure with distinct faces — rather than massive or platy material.

pH

Almonds prefer a slightly acidic to neutral range, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.5 measured in water. They tolerate mildly alkaline conditions, which is fortunate because many semi-arid soils are calcareous and alkaline.

The practical issues at the margins:

  • Above about pH 7.5–8.0, availability of iron, zinc and manganese declines. Lime-induced iron chlorosis is a common and persistent problem on calcareous soils, managed through rootstock selection and chelated micronutrient application — managed, not solved.
  • Below about pH 5.5, aluminium and manganese availability rises toward toxicity and calcium and magnesium availability falls.

pH is measurable cheaply and should be measured at more than one depth. Surface pH and subsoil pH frequently differ, and it is the subsoil the roots will occupy.

Salinity

Almonds are relatively salt-sensitive compared with many tree crops, which makes salinity a first-order consideration on irrigated semi-arid land rather than a secondary one.

Two sources, and both need assessing:

Existing soil salinity, measured as electrical conductivity of a saturation extract, at multiple depths. Salts frequently accumulate at depth or in specific positions in the landscape, so a surface sample is not sufficient.

Salinity introduced by irrigation water. Every irrigation applies salt. In a climate without enough rainfall to leach it, that salt accumulates in the root zone unless a leaching fraction is deliberately applied. Irrigation water perfectly acceptable in a humid climate — where winter rain flushes the profile annually — can be unusable in a semi-arid one.

This is the slow failure mode of semi-arid irrigated agriculture: the orchard performs for years, then declines, and by the time the cause is obvious the salt is in the profile.

Practical requirements: test both soil and water before planting; design a leaching requirement into the irrigation system where water quality demands it; ensure drainage exists to carry leached water away, because leaching without drainage just relocates the problem; and monitor soil salinity over time rather than assuming the initial assessment holds.

Sodicity

Distinct from salinity and often overlooked. Sodic soils have a high proportion of exchangeable sodium relative to calcium and magnesium, which disperses clay aggregates. Dispersed clay blocks pores, so the soil sets hard when dry, seals when wet, and infiltrates very poorly.

Sodicity is the reason the pit must record what lies below a restriction. Deep ripping into sodic subsoil, or mixing it upward, can produce soil physically worse than before — dispersive, structureless material in the root zone.

Sodic subsoil is common in semi-arid landscapes. It is measurable, it changes the soil-preparation decision fundamentally, and it is invisible from the surface.

Amelioration with gypsum is possible where sodicity is moderate, but it is a long-term programme requiring significant material, and it needs to be planned as part of establishment rather than discovered afterwards.

Stones

Stones affect almond orchards through the harvest chain more than through tree performance. Mechanical harvesting picks nuts off the orchard floor; stones on that floor enter the harvested product, requiring additional cleaning and causing wear in processing equipment.

Stones also increase wear substantially in deep tillage, and stony ground makes depth control harder.

Assess stone content at the surface and through the profile, and budget for surface stone removal as part of establishment if the harvest method requires it.

An assessment checklist

Before committing to a planting, in this order:

  1. Water — quantity against peak demand, quality, legal security, reliability in the driest year. A "no" here stops the project.
  2. Frost risk at bloom — almonds flower very early; in a continental climate this is the dominant yield risk. Site topography and cold-air drainage matter more than mean temperature.
  3. Profile depth and restrictions — pits, multiple locations, with depths recorded
  4. Drainage — profile evidence, landscape position, water table
  5. Texture and structure at each horizon
  6. pH at multiple depths
  7. Salinity — soil at multiple depths, and irrigation water
  8. Sodicity — particularly the material below any restriction
  9. Stones — surface and profile
  10. Trafficability and slope for the machinery the crop requires

Items 1 and 2 are the ones most often answered optimistically, and the ones that most often end projects.

References and further reading

Almond soil, pH, salinity and sodicity tolerances above are consistent with published horticultural guidance from major almond-producing regions and with standard soil-assessment practice. Growers should confirm specific tolerance thresholds and rootstock recommendations against current regional extension material for their own conditions and rootstock selection.

item.title: Building a Large-Scale Almond Production and Processing Value Chain
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
The problem

Georgian horticulture has a structural gap between growing and value capture. Producers grow well and sell unprocessed, which puts them at the thinnest margin in the chain. The processing value — hulling, shelling, drying, sorting, grading, and everything beyond — is captured elsewhere, usually outside the country.

For a large orchard this is an existential issue rather than an inefficiency. An orchard of a few thousand hectares reaching full bearing produces a volume that cannot be sold unprocessed at an acceptable price. The processing capacity has to exist by the time the trees bear, or the orchard investment does not return.

Direction of planning

The counter-intuitive part, and the thing most often got backwards: processing capacity determines the harvest calendar, not the reverse.

Almonds come off in a short window and must be dried quickly to a safe moisture content. If receiving and drying capacity is below field output, either the field stops or product waits in conditions where quality degrades and aflatoxin risk rises. The first is expensive; the second is a food-safety failure.

So the chain is planned backward:

processing throughput
   → harvest rate the facility can absorb
      → harvest machinery and transport fleet required
         → area that can be brought to bearing this year

Planning it forward — plant the area, then work out how to process the crop — is how orchards end up selling in-shell at commodity prices.

Orchard side

EastFruit (2021) and Investor.ge (2022) report approximately 2,300 hectares of almond orchard developed from 2017, with more than 675,000 trees of Spanish and Italian origin. EastFruit reports varieties including Guara, Supernova and Lauren, with Guara and Supernova designated for European export, and fruit calibre of 29–30 mm.

Two decisions there are worth drawing out.

Self-fertile varieties. Guara and Supernova are self-fertile. At scale, in a continental climate with spring frost risk, that removes dependence on pollinator block layout and on bee activity during a narrow and possibly cold bloom window. It is a significant de-risking of the crop, decided once, permanently, at planting.

Variety chosen against a market specification. Designating specific varieties for European export means the market requirement — calibre, shape, kernel characteristics — drove the planting decision rather than being discovered afterwards. That is the right order, and it only works if the target market is identified before the trees are ordered.

See Almond Orchard Development.

Primary processing

EastFruit reported in 2021 that new equipment would allow drying and shelling to be carried out in-house, rather than the crop leaving the operation unprocessed.

The functions involved: receiving, hulling and shelling, drying, cleaning and sizing, sorting, and controlled storage.

Of these, drying is the one that cannot be compromised. It is the food-safety step, and drying capacity rather than shelling capacity is frequently the real constraint on how fast the harvest can run. Storage matters commercially in a different way: it converts a harvest-time surplus into year-round sales instead of a forced sale at harvest prices.

Capacity, investment and equipment figures are not published here.

  • Published capacity (EastFruit, September 2021): 2.5 tonnes per hour.
  • Figure in my own professional record: approximately 14–15 tonnes per hour.

These differ by roughly six times. They may measure different things — in-hull intake versus kernel throughput, or an initial line versus a later expansion — but until a specification sheet establishes which, neither is presented here as the operation's capacity.

Similarly withheld: a processing investment figure of approximately USD 15 million (no published source isolates processing capex; Investor.ge reports GEL 150 million for the operation as a whole, a different quantity), and the equipment manufacturer's name (published sources spell it differently, and two real manufacturers match the different spellings).

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: equipment specification sheet, commissioning report, machine nameplate photograph, audited capital accounts]

Secondary processing

Secondary processing converts kernel into products with longer shelf life and different market channels — flour, oil and milk among them.

The economic argument is about the product that fails whole-kernel specification. Every orchard produces a proportion of broken, undersized or cosmetically imperfect kernel that is entirely good food but cannot be sold as premium whole kernel. Without secondary processing, that fraction is sold at a discount. With it, the discount becomes a raw-material cost for a higher-value product.

This changes the economics of the whole operation and — importantly — reduces the pressure to hit unrealistic export-grade percentages, which in turn reduces the temptation to cut corners in sorting.

Export preparation

EastFruit reports export-oriented production with varieties designated for European markets. A Caucasus Business Week interview refers to Europe and Gulf countries as targets.

EU market access is a systems requirement: maximum residue levels determined by the orchard spray programme years in advance; aflatoxin control through harvest timing, rapid drying, storage and sorting; traceability from block to consignment; HACCP-compliant facility design; and audit-ready documentation.

Almost all of it is decided upstream — in the orchard and in the facility's design. Very little can be corrected at the point of shipment.

This site does not claim completed and audited export shipments. Export-oriented production and variety selection for European markets are documented. Delivered shipments are not.

The two published 2021 figures illustrate why forecasts and results are kept separate here: EastFruit reported a forecast of 500–600 tonnes in September 2021; Investor.ge reported an 800-tonne in-shell crop the following April. Neither is presented as the other.

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: export declarations, phytosanitary certificates, buyer confirmations]

Regional processing for independent growers

EastFruit reported that management intended to offer processing services to other Georgian almond and walnut growers, with a view to establishing a regional processing base.

This is the part of the project with the widest effect. A grower with a few hectares cannot justify hulling, drying and sorting equipment. Without access to it the crop sells unprocessed at the lowest margin — so quality is not worth investing in, and the regional crop stays low value in aggregate. That is a trap that individual effort cannot escape.

Accessible regional processing changes the arithmetic: quality becomes worth achieving because it becomes sellable. The benefit accrues to growers who have no relationship with the company beyond using the facility.

Published sources record this as a stated intention. This site does not claim the service was delivered at scale or state how many growers used it. [VERIFICATION REQUIRED: service records, grower agreements, throughput data]

Standards and certification

The Chemonics/USAID Zrda Activity technical brief on GeoGAP (October 2021) quotes me on the role of certification in market access, and records that Adjara Group planned to earn GeoGAP certification at its almond orchard, berry farm and vineyard.

"Now, when buying GeoGAP-certified products, we have a guarantee that they are locally grown, safe (in terms of chemical and biological contamination), traceable, and environmentally friendly."

Chemonics / USAID Zrda Activity, A Local Certification System in Georgia, October 2021

Documented as a plan. This site does not claim the certification was achieved.

What was hard

Matching capacity growth to orchard growth. Orchard area expands with a planting decision; processing capacity expands through a capital project with a long lead time. Keeping them aligned means committing to processing investment against a bearing area that does not exist yet — which is uncomfortable and necessary.

Drying capacity being the real constraint. It is easy to specify a facility around shelling throughput, because that is the number people quote. Drying is what limits how fast harvest can run and is the step where compromise creates a food-safety problem rather than an efficiency loss.

Quality consistency across blocks planted years apart. Different crews, different conditions, different levels of establishment care. It shows up at harvest as variable maturity and variable yield within a nominally uniform planting.

The forecast-versus-result gap. Publicly stated harvest forecasts and reported outcomes for 2021 differ substantially. That is a normal feature of a young orchard, and it is a good argument for not publishing forecasts as though they were results — a discipline this site applies retrospectively.

item.title: Developing Commercial Agriculture in Georgia's Semi-Arid Udabno Region
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
The site

Udabno lies in the Sagarejo district of Kakheti, in eastern Georgia. The name means "desert" in Georgian, which is a fair description of the starting condition: low rainfall, high summer temperatures, sparse vegetation cover, erodible soils, and no history of intensive commercial horticulture.

Land like this is available and cheap for a reason. Every input a horticultural operation depends on — water, power, roads, workable soil — either did not exist or existed inadequately. The development problem was therefore not "how do we grow almonds here" but "what has to be built before growing almonds here is possible".

Scale — and a disagreement in the record

The operation is publicly reported as working a substantial landholding, and the published figures do not agree with each other:

This site does not resolve that spread by choosing the largest number. The likeliest explanation is that the figures describe different quantities — total territory held, land acquired, and land under active cultivation — but until a land-registry extract or audited company record establishes which is which, no total-area figure is used in any headline claim here.

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: land-registry extract or audited company records separating land owned, leased and under active cultivation]

The almond orchard figure is better supported: approximately 2,300 hectares, reported independently by both EastFruit (2021) and Investor.ge (2022), with more than 675,000 trees of Spanish and Italian origin.

What the work involved

Soil assessment

The first task was establishing what the soil actually was, block by block, rather than what regional survey data suggested. That means pits — dug, described, photographed, and interpreted.

The recurring finding on land of this type is a dense subsoil layer that roots will not enter. It may be geological, or the result of long-term consolidation under extensive grazing. Either way it sets a ceiling on rooting volume, and in a semi-arid climate a shallow rooting volume means the trees depend entirely on irrigation frequency, with no buffer.

The gap between the soil map and the pit was larger and more frequent than I expected at the outset. Blocks that mapped as similar behaved differently; blocks that mapped as poor were sometimes fine below 60 cm. We moved to treating survey data as a sampling plan rather than a finding — it told us where to dig, not what we would find.

That change cost time early and saved considerably more later, because it stopped us specifying uniform treatment across ground that was not uniform.

Subsoil preparation

Where assessment confirmed a restriction, it was opened mechanically before planting. This is the least reversible decision in the whole project: once trees are in, the subsoil is inaccessible for twenty-five years.

The technical reasoning is set out in full on Deep-Ripping and Soil Preparation.

Project-specific ripping parameters — working depths, machine specifications, areas treated, contractor names and measured results — are not published, pending documentation. [VERIFICATION REQUIRED: dated work records, machinery specifications, soil profile descriptions, photographs, contractor consent]

Water

Nothing else was possible without this. The work covered source development, storage to buffer supply variability against a strongly seasonal demand curve, mainline and distribution construction, filtration, and fertigation capability.

Two design points proved decisive. First, sizing against peak demand during nut fill rather than average annual demand — a system adequate on average fails at the exact moment yield is set. Second, designing for distribution uniformity and then actually measuring it in service, because uniformity degrades through emitter blockage and pressure variation and the degradation is invisible from a vehicle.

See Irrigation and Agricultural Infrastructure.

Erosion control

On erodible semi-arid soil, every operation that disturbs the surface creates exposure. Alignment was the primary control: rip lines, rows and traffic lanes across the slope rather than down it, because a rip line running downhill is a drain and, on this soil, the beginning of a gully.

Beyond alignment: permanent inter-row cover where the water budget allowed, treatment of the specific points where water concentrates — road edges, culvert outlets, headlands, block corners — and an operational rule against cultivating dry bare soil in wind.

See Reducing Erosion in Semi-Arid Agricultural Land.

Infrastructure

Roads capable of carrying loaded harvest traffic in all weather; turning and loading areas sized for harvest machinery; workshop, fuel and storage facilities; staff facilities; and power.

Investor.ge records this in my own words at the time: "Before Udabno started business in Kakheti there was no internet and television in the local village. We built high voltage electrical lines." The same report notes support provided to local schools and kindergartens.

That is worth stating plainly because it is easy to underestimate: an agricultural project on undeveloped land ends up building public infrastructure, because the project cannot function without it and nobody else is going to.

Mechanization

Machinery capable of working heavy, dry, compacted ground — with the accompanying problem that the mass required for traction in deep tillage causes compaction in every other operation. Segregating heavy work from routine work is part of the design rather than an afterthought.

See Agricultural Mechanization.

Mixed production

The operation was not almonds alone. Investor.ge reports approximately 150,000 nursery rootstocks, livestock of 74 buffalo, 285 cows and 1,500 sheep, and extensive berry, vegetable and vine production. A Caucasus Business Week interview also refers to wheat, including Georgian endemic varieties.

Mixed production on a project like this is partly risk management — a perennial crop takes years to bear, and annual crops and livestock generate revenue and occupy the workforce meanwhile — and partly agronomic, since livestock integration and rotation contribute to the soil work.

Employment

Published figures differ. A Caucasus Business Week interview gives 150 permanent and 200–500 seasonal employees; Investor.ge reports "over 300 people per season" in the Sagarejo region. Both are reported here rather than averaged into a single convenient number.

What did not work first time

A case study without this section is marketing.

Treating mapped soil as known soil. Corrected early, but it cost time and produced specifications for uniform treatment on non-uniform ground.

Underestimating infrastructure lead times. Roads, power and workshop capacity were treated as supporting work while planting was the priority. They then became the constraint on operations for longer than they should have. Infrastructure deferred is infrastructure that limits you later, at higher cost.

Sequencing planting against nursery supply rather than irrigation readiness. When trees arrive on the nursery's schedule and irrigation is on the construction schedule, blocks get planted before they can be watered properly. First-year establishment suffers, and the effect stays visible in the canopy for years. The fix is to phase planting against infrastructure and accept holding or losing nursery stock instead — a smaller cost, paid once.

Assuming pilot-block performance would scale. Pilot blocks get the best land, the most attention and the most experienced people. Cost and quality figures derived from them are optimistic for the full-scale operation.

Outcome

An almond orchard of approximately 2,300 hectares developed from 2017, with irrigation infrastructure, mechanization capability, processing capacity and supporting infrastructure — on land that had not previously supported intensive commercial horticulture.

During the period of my leadership, Udabno Group's "Udabno Regenerative Transition" project was named the SME-category winner under SDG 12 at the 2023 Corporate Responsibility Award — Business for SDGs (UN Global Compact Network Georgia, 12 October 2023). An organisational award to the project team.

item.title: About Goderdzi Metreveli
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Goderdzi Metreveli is a Georgian agricultural executive and engineering professional whose work has centred on the development of commercial agriculture in the semi-arid Sagarejo district of Kakheti, in eastern Georgia.

His name is associated in independent publications with the Udabno agricultural operation, part of Adjara Group. Reporting by EastFruit in September 2021 and by Investor.ge in April 2022 identifies him as Director of Udabno. A technical brief published in October 2021 by Chemonics under the USAID-funded Zrda Activity quotes him as Managing Director of Adjara Group. A Caucasus Business Week interview describes him as Director of Udabno Shelling, the operation's processing arm.

Working in a semi-arid environment

Udabno is a low-rainfall, erosion-prone landscape that had not previously supported intensive commercial horticulture. That is not an incidental detail — it determines the whole shape of the work. Land that has never been irrigated has no water infrastructure. Land that has never been cropped intensively often has a dense, poorly structured subsoil that will not admit roots. Land with thin vegetation cover and summer wind loses topsoil the moment it is disturbed.

Converting it meant working on several fronts at once: assessing soil profiles and identifying restrictive layers, opening those layers mechanically before planting, establishing water supply and distribution where none existed, building roads and operational buildings, and selecting machinery capable of working heavy, dry ground without compacting it further.

My own focus within that work has been the decisions taken before planting. Soil-profile assessment, subsoil preparation, row alignment, drainage and irrigation layout are all things that constrain an orchard for its entire productive life and are expensive or impossible to revisit once trees are in the ground. Getting them wrong is not a setback that can be corrected in a later season; it is a permanent reduction in what the block can do.

Almond orchard development

EastFruit (2021) and Investor.ge (2022) report the Udabno almond orchard as covering approximately 2,300 hectares, developed from 2017, with more than 675,000 trees of Spanish and Italian origin. EastFruit reports the varieties in production as including Guara, Supernova and Lauren — Guara and Supernova designated for European export — with fruit calibre in the 29–30 mm range.

At that scale the difficult problems are rarely horticultural. They are problems of sequencing and matching: planting no faster than the irrigation system being built alongside can serve; sizing harvest capacity against processing capacity rather than against orchard area; and keeping establishment quality consistent across blocks planted years apart by different crews under different conditions.

Processing and the value chain

The operation developed both primary and secondary almond-processing capacity. EastFruit reported in 2021 that new equipment would allow drying and shelling to be done in-house, and that management intended to offer processing services to other Georgian almond and walnut growers.

That last point addresses a structural problem in Georgian horticulture. Most producers are too small to justify processing equipment of their own, so they sell unprocessed and capture the lowest margin in the chain. Regional processing capacity that independent growers can access changes what their crop is worth, which is a different kind of outcome from expanding a single company's own orchard.

Standards and market access

I have contributed publicly to the discussion of agricultural standards in Georgia. The Chemonics/USAID technical brief on the GeoGAP certification scheme quotes my view of why a locally appropriate standard matters:

"In general, we think that implementation of GeoGAP standards, and going through certification, will give farmers [the] ability to also sell their products at higher prices in the retail sector."

Chemonics / USAID Zrda Activity, A Local Certification System in Georgia, October 2021

International certification schemes are export-oriented, expensive and demanding. Most Georgian producers cannot reach them, and the ones who can sell to exporters to recoup the cost. That leaves a gap: growers who want to demonstrate quality but cannot afford an international scheme, and domestic buyers who would pay a premium if there were anything to verify it. A locally calibrated standard is a step onto that ladder rather than a substitute for the top of it.

Regenerative transition

During the period of my leadership, Udabno Group's "Udabno Regenerative Transition" project was named the SME-category winner under Sustainable Development Goal 12 at the 2023 Corporate Responsibility Award — Business for SDGs, announced by UN Global Compact Network Georgia on 12 October 2023.

This was an award to the organisation and its project team. It is recorded here because the project is relevant to the work described on this site, not as a personal distinction.

How I work

The projects described on this site were delivered by teams — agronomists, engineers, machine operators, contractors, consultants and partner organisations. What is described here is my role within that shared work.

The habit that has served best is measuring rather than assuming. A soil map is a hypothesis; a pit dug in the block is evidence, and the two disagree more often than people expect. A machinery configuration that works in one soil type may smear and seal in another 400 metres away. Testing on one block before committing a fleet costs a few days and has repeatedly saved seasons.

Several items from my own professional record are deliberately not published here pending documentation — including specific employment dates and titles, total landholding area, processing capacity and investment figures, and education details. The reasoning for each is recorded in the site's fact-verification report.

item.content:encoded:
Every figure on this page carries its source. Where published accounts disagree, that is stated rather than resolved in the flattering direction. Where an achievement belongs to an organisation, it is described as an organisational achievement.

1. Semi-arid land development

Udabno, in the Sagarejo district of Kakheti, is low-rainfall, erosion-prone land that had not previously supported intensive commercial horticulture. From 2017 onward it was developed into a working agricultural operation.

I held a senior leadership role within that operation — identified in independent reporting as its Director during 2021–2022. The operation is publicly reported as controlling or managing a substantial landholding, and I want to be precise about that figure because published accounts do not agree:

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: land-registry or audited company records separating land owned, leased and under active cultivation]

Until that is resolved, no total-area figure appears in the headline claims on this site. The likeliest explanation is that these figures describe different things — total territory, land acquired, and land under cultivation — but until a document confirms which is which, publishing the largest number would be misleading.

What the work involved is not in dispute: land preparation and subsoil opening, water-supply and irrigation infrastructure built where none existed, orchard establishment, annual crop production, soil protection and erosion mitigation, farm roads and operational buildings, and agricultural mechanization suited to heavy dry ground.

No individual transformed this land. It was done by multidisciplinary teams of agronomists, engineers, operators, contractors and partner organisations.

2. Large-scale almond orchard development

EastFruit (September 2021) and Investor.ge (April 2022) both report the Udabno almond orchard at approximately 2,300 hectares, developed from 2017, with more than 675,000 trees of Spanish and Italian origin.

EastFruit reports varieties including Guara, Supernova and Lauren, with Guara and Supernova designated for European export, and fruit calibre of 29–30 mm.

Work covered orchard planning and block layout, variety selection where documented, soil preparation before planting, irrigation design and installation, harvest planning, machinery specification, organic-transition objectives, and preparation for European market requirements.

The consistent difficulty at this scale is matching rates. Planting can outrun irrigation construction; harvest capacity can outrun processing capacity; establishment quality can drift between blocks planted years apart. Most of the management effort goes into keeping those in step rather than into any single technical decision.

3. Almond processing and value-chain development

The operation developed both primary and secondary almond-processing capacity. EastFruit reported in 2021 that new equipment would enable drying and shelling in-house, and that management intended to offer processing services to other Georgian almond and walnut growers — with a view to a regional processing base.

That intention matters more than it might appear. Most Georgian nut producers are too small to justify their own processing equipment, so they sell unprocessed and take the thinnest margin in the chain. Accessible regional processing changes what an independent grower's crop is worth.

Figures held back. My professional record includes a processing investment of approximately USD 15 million, capacity of approximately 14–15 tonnes per hour, and a named equipment manufacturer. None is published here:

  • The only published capacity figure is 2.5 tonnes per hour (EastFruit, 2021) — roughly a sixth of the figure in my record. The two may measure different things: in-hull intake versus kernel throughput, or an original line versus a later expansion. Until a specification sheet says which, neither figure should be presented as the site's own.
  • No published source isolates processing capital expenditure. Investor.ge reports GEL 150 million invested in the Udabno operation as a whole, which is a different quantity.
  • Sources spell the equipment manufacturer differently, and two real manufacturers match the different spellings.

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: equipment specification sheet, commissioning report, machine nameplate photograph, audited capital accounts]

4. European export preparation

EastFruit reports that Guara and Supernova plantings were designated for European export, and that the operation was developing export-oriented production. A Caucasus Business Week interview refers to Europe and Gulf countries as target markets.

What is claimed here: export-oriented production developed and targeted at European markets, with variety selection made accordingly.

What is not claimed here: completed and audited export shipments. Harvest forecasts are not production results, and the two published figures for 2021 illustrate why — EastFruit reported a forecast of 500–600 tonnes in September 2021, while Investor.ge reported an 800-tonne in-shell crop the following April. Forecast and outcome are separate facts and are not merged on this site.

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: export declarations, phytosanitary certificates, buyer confirmations]

5. Regenerative transition and eco-innovation

Work in this area covered reduced environmental impact, organic-transition planning, irrigation efficiency under constrained water supply, improved nutrient management, erosion mitigation, lower chemical-input objectives, zero-waste and circular-production concepts, and — the constraint that makes the rest difficult — commercial viability throughout.

Regenerative practice at commercial scale is not the same discipline as regenerative practice on a smallholding. The techniques are similar; the constraints are not. A 2,000-hectare orchard cannot adopt a practice that halves throughput during the harvest window, however good it is for the soil, and a practice that cannot survive a bad year will not survive at all.

Udabno Group's "Udabno Regenerative Transition" project was named the SME-category winner under Sustainable Development Goal 12 at the 2023 Corporate Responsibility Award — Business for SDGs, announced by UN Global Compact Network Georgia on 12 October 2023.

This was an award to the organisation and its project team, made during the period of my leadership. It was not a personal award. The same announcement names individual honourees separately under its SDG Pioneer category, and I was not among them.

The ceremony was held at the Rustaveli Theatre with support from the Government of Sweden, USAID's Civil Society Engagement Program and the Council of Europe Office; entries were judged in large-business and SME categories by a jury of Georgian and international members.

On organic certification: this site does not claim certified organic production. EastFruit reported in 2021 that the company planned transition to certified organic production "in a few years"; a Caucasus Business Week interview records my own description of the growing method as using "no preparations, whether organic or otherwise". "Organic" is a legally protected term in both Georgian and EU marketing law, and it is not used here without a certificate.

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: organic certificate number, certifying body, scope, validity]

6. GeoGAP and market standards

The Chemonics/USAID Zrda Activity technical brief on GeoGAP (October 2021) quotes me twice by name and title on the value of the scheme:

"Now, when buying GeoGAP-certified products, we have a guarantee that they are locally grown, safe (in terms of chemical and biological contamination), traceable, and environmentally friendly."

The same brief records that Adjara Group planned to implement good agricultural practices and earn GeoGAP certification at its almond orchard, berry farm and vineyard. That is documented as a plan; this site does not claim the certification was achieved.

GeoGAP was created by the Georgian Farmers' Association with USAID and Chemonics support as a scaled-down, locally calibrated stepping-stone toward international schemes such as GLOBALG.A.P. Its value is precisely that it is achievable: an export-grade scheme that no domestic producer can afford does nothing for the domestic market.

7. USAID and international partnership context

USAID and Adjara Group signed a Memorandum of Understanding on 21 July 2021, affirming a commitment to jointly advancing sustainable and inclusive economic development. The MOU covered competitiveness in hospitality, creative industries and agriculture, with attention to workforce development, inclusive employment, local business support, produce sourcing and sustainable tourism in Abastumani and Samtskhe-Javakheti. It was signed by USAID/Georgia Mission Director Peter Wiebler and directors of Adjara Group.

I am not named in the announcement of that memorandum, and this site does not state or imply that I signed it. The published scope is also geographically focused on Abastumani and Samtskhe-Javakheti rather than on Udabno, and it should not be read as a partnership about the almond project.

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: for any personal role in the MOU — a photograph, the signed document, or an official publication naming me]

My separate trainer role in a U.S.-supported development programme also remains unverified pending the programme name, dates and supporting documents.

8. Deep-ripping and soil-preparation expertise

This is the area of the work I know best and the area where I can publish least, because none of the project-specific parameters has supporting documentation attached to it yet.

Held pending evidence: single-shank configuration, working depths, tractor horsepower, areas treated, contractor names, and measured results. [VERIFICATION REQUIRED: dated work records, machinery specifications, soil profiles, photographs, contractor documentation and consent]

What is published instead is the technical reasoning itself, which does not depend on disclosing project data: Deep-Ripping and Soil Preparation for Orchard Establishment and the supporting articles on identifying restrictive layers, soil moisture, depth, spacing and direction, the distinction from subsoiling and common mistakes.

A note on how this page is written

Achievements attributed to an organisation are described as organisational. Figures carry sources. Contradictions between sources are shown rather than resolved silently. Items lacking documentation are marked and withheld.

This makes for a less emphatic page than the alternative. It also makes it one that holds up when checked — which, for a professional record, is the only property that matters.

item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Five areas, each with a detailed page and a cluster of technical articles behind it. They are not independent — the reason deep ripping matters is that it determines what irrigation can achieve, and the reason processing capacity matters is that it determines when the orchard can be harvested. The interdependence is the point.

Regenerative Agriculture in Semi-Arid Georgia

Restoring soil function on low-rainfall, low-organic-matter land while the operation stays commercially viable. Erosion control, organic-transition planning, nutrient management, irrigation efficiency, and how to measure improvement in something other than yield.

The hard constraint is that a practice which cannot survive a bad season will not be adopted, however sound the soil science behind it.

Almond Orchard Development

Planning and establishing commercial almond orchards: site assessment, variety selection for continental and semi-arid conditions, block layout, planting sequence, irrigation design, harvest planning and machinery requirements.

At scale, the binding problems are sequencing problems — keeping planting, irrigation construction, harvest capacity and processing capacity in step with each other.

Deep-Ripping and Soil Preparation

Identifying restrictive soil layers and deciding whether to open them; the distinction between subsoiling and deep ripping; soil-moisture requirements; depth, spacing and direction; the relationship to drainage and irrigation; post-ripping settlement; and the cases where ripping should not be done at all.

The most consequential and least reversible decision in orchard establishment, and the one most often made on assumption rather than evidence.

Irrigation and Agricultural Infrastructure

Engineering productive agricultural systems where water is the binding constraint: source development, storage, distribution, filtration and fertigation, scheduling under limited supply, drainage, and the roads and buildings a large operation depends on.

Also: Agricultural Mechanization — fleet specification for heavy soils, matching implement to condition, and harvest machinery chains.

Almond Processing and Export Development

Primary and secondary processing, matching throughput to harvest logistics, quality standards for European markets, GeoGAP and commercial market access, and regional processing capacity that independent growers can use.

Consulting and training

If you are establishing an orchard on difficult ground, planning soil preparation, sizing irrigation or mechanization, or assessing a processing value chain, get in touch. Enquiries are welcome in Georgian and English.

item.title: Agricultural Mechanization
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Mechanization decisions on a large operation are usually discussed as procurement. They are better understood as capability decisions: the machinery available determines what soil preparation is physically possible, which determines what the site can become.

On heavy, dry, compacted ground this is not a marginal effect. If the available traction cannot pull a ripper through a restrictive layer at the required depth, that layer stays, and the orchard's rooting volume is permanently limited — not by agronomy, but by the equipment on hand when the decision was made.

Selection principles

Match the machine to the soil, not to the brochure. Manufacturer performance figures are established under favourable conditions. Draught requirements in dry, hard, stony ground are substantially higher than in the conditions used for specification, and progress rates correspondingly lower.

Power is necessary but not sufficient. Deep tillage needs drawbar pull, which requires weight, appropriate ballast, tyre or track configuration and adequate traction. Engine power that cannot be transmitted to the ground is not useful. This is why tracked or heavily ballasted machines earn their cost in deep-ripping work while a nominally similar wheeled tractor cannot do the job.

Weight is a liability outside the job it is needed for. The same mass that provides traction for ripping causes compaction in every other operation. A fleet built entirely around the heaviest task compacts the soil it was bought to improve. Segregating heavy work from routine work — by machine, by traffic lane, and by timing — is part of the design.

Controlled traffic where practical. Confining compaction to permanent lanes protects the rest of the block. In orchards this is largely automatic once rows are established, which makes the alignment decisions at establishment more consequential than they appear.

Serviceability in the actual location. A machine that cannot be repaired locally within the harvest window is a risk regardless of its specification. Parts availability, dealer support and the skill base to maintain it matter as much as its capability. In a market without an established machinery base, this frequently outranks performance.

Detail (scheduled): Selecting High-Horsepower Farm Machinery

Implement matching

The implement, not the tractor, does the work, and matching it to soil condition is where results are won or lost.

  • Ripper configuration — shank number, spacing, geometry and wear parts, matched to the depth and the soil. See Deep-Ripping and Soil Preparation.
  • Wear parts as a consumable. In stony ground, wear is a major operating cost and worn points change the geometry of the work: a blunt shank smears where a sharp one fractures. Wear affects results, not just cost.
  • Depth control. Consistency matters more than maximum depth. Variable depth leaves untreated columns.
  • Matching to moisture. The same implement in the same soil produces fracture or smearing depending on moisture. See Correct Soil Moisture for Deep Ripping.

Harvest machinery

Mechanical almond harvest is a chain — shake, sweep, pick up, transport, receive — and it runs at the speed of its slowest element.

  • Trunk or canopy shakers removing the crop
  • Sweepers windrowing from the orchard floor
  • Pick-up machines collecting the windrow
  • Transport to the processing facility
  • Receiving and drying capacity

The failure mode is capacity mismatch. An additional shaker adds nothing if the pick-up machinery or the receiving facility is already the constraint — it just moves the queue. Fleet sizing has to be calculated backward from processing throughput, not forward from orchard area.

Orchard floor condition determines harvest efficiency and product cleanliness. It is a decision made at establishment: levelling, stone management, surface shaping. An uneven floor costs harvest efficiency and product quality every season for the orchard's life, and cannot be meaningfully improved once trees are in.

See Machinery Requirements for Large Almond Operations.

Maintenance capability

On a large operation, maintenance capability is part of the machinery decision.

  • Workshop capacity proportionate to the fleet
  • Parts inventory for critical failures during harvest, when a delay is not recoverable within the season
  • Operator training — the same machine in different hands produces measurably different work, and in deep tillage the difference is large
  • Scheduled maintenance timed against the operational calendar, so it happens before the window rather than during it
  • Records to inform replacement decisions with data rather than impression

Operator skill is consistently underweighted in mechanization planning. In deep ripping the operator controls depth consistency, speed, and the judgement about whether conditions are right at all — and that judgement is the one that decides whether the pass fractures the soil or smears it. Training operators to read the soil behind the machine, and giving them the authority to stop when it looks wrong, produced better outcomes than any equipment upgrade.

Consulting

Engagements are practical rather than advisory-in-the-abstract. The most useful work usually happens before planting, when decisions are still open.

Site assessment before establishment. Soil-profile survey, identification of restrictive layers, drainage assessment, and an honest answer on whether the site suits the crop being proposed. Sometimes that answer is no, and it is cheaper to hear it at this stage than in year six.

Soil-preparation specification. Whether deep ripping is justified; if so, at what depth, spacing, direction and soil moisture; what machinery is required; and how the work should be sequenced against drainage and irrigation installation.

Irrigation and infrastructure planning. Source, storage, distribution, filtration and fertigation; scheduling under constrained supply; and phasing construction against planting.

Mechanization strategy. Fleet specification for heavy or compacted soils, implement matching, harvest machinery chains, and maintenance capability.

Processing and value-chain assessment. Matching processing throughput to harvest logistics; assessing whether regional processing is viable.

Second opinion on an existing plan. Frequently the highest-value engagement: reviewing a specification someone else has produced, before capital is committed.

Training

Delivered to farm teams, machine operators, agronomists and agricultural students. Practical, in-field where possible.

  • Reading a soil profile: digging, describing and interpreting a pit
  • Identifying restrictive layers and deciding whether to treat them
  • Assessing soil moisture for tillage decisions — by hand, in the field
  • Deep-ripping operations: setup, depth control, direction, quality checking
  • Machinery selection and implement matching for heavy soils
  • Orchard establishment quality control
  • Irrigation system operation and maintenance
  • Erosion recognition and mitigation

The soil-pit session is the one that changes how people work. Most operators have never seen the layer they have been working above.

Topics:

  • Regenerative practice at commercial scale, and its real constraints
  • What we get wrong about soil preparation
  • Building an agricultural value chain in a market without one

item.title: Planning and Managing Large-Scale Almond Orchards
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
An almond orchard of a few hectares is a horticultural project. An almond orchard of a few thousand hectares is a logistics and infrastructure project that happens to grow almonds. The agronomy is largely known; what determines the outcome is whether planting, irrigation construction, harvest capacity and processing capacity stay in step with one another.

EastFruit (2021) and Investor.ge (2022) report the Udabno orchard at approximately 2,300 hectares, developed from 2017, with more than 675,000 trees of Spanish and Italian origin, and varieties including Guara, Supernova and Lauren.

Site assessment before commitment

The questions that decide whether a site should be planted at all, in order:

  1. Is there secure water, in sufficient quantity, of adequate quality? Almonds are a high-water-requirement crop with no dormant tolerance for drought during nut fill. A site without secure water is not an almond site, whatever else is in its favour. Water quality matters as much as quantity — salinity limits are real and almonds are relatively sensitive.
  2. Is the soil deep enough, and can it be made deep enough? See below.
  3. Does the site drain? Almonds are intolerant of waterlogging and susceptible to root and crown diseases in poorly drained ground.
  4. What is the frost risk at bloom? Almonds flower very early. In continental climates this is the dominant yield risk. Cold-air drainage and site topography matter more than mean temperature statistics.
  5. Is the ground workable by the machinery the crop requires? Mechanical harvesting needs a firm, level, well-shaped orchard floor. Slope, stoniness and surface irregularity are harvest constraints, not just establishment ones.

A "no" to question 1 or 4 should stop the project. In practice these are the questions most often answered optimistically.

Soil requirements and preparation

Almonds want deep, well-drained soil with no restriction in the rooting zone. They are unusually unforgiving of two conditions: waterlogging, and a shallow restrictive layer in a climate where the tree depends on stored soil water between irrigations.

Which means: the soil work happens before planting, or it does not happen. Profile assessment by pit, identification of restrictive layers, deep ripping where justified, drainage where required, then levelling and irrigation.

See Deep-Ripping and Soil Preparation and Soil Requirements for Commercial Almond Orchards.

Variety selection in continental and semi-arid conditions

EastFruit reports Guara, Supernova and Lauren among the varieties in production at Udabno, with Guara and Supernova designated for European export and fruit calibre of 29–30 mm.

The selection criteria that matter in a continental climate:

  • Bloom timing. Later bloom reduces frost exposure. In a climate with spring frost risk this is the single most important varietal characteristic, ahead of yield potential.
  • Self-fertility. Self-fertile varieties such as Guara and Supernova remove dependence on pollinator layout and on bee activity during a narrow, possibly cold, bloom window. At scale this substantially de-risks the crop.
  • Kernel characteristics for the target market. European buyers specify calibre, shape, colour and shell characteristics. Variety choice is a market decision as much as an agronomic one, and it is made once for twenty-five years.
  • Harvest timing spread. Multiple varieties with staggered maturity spread the load on harvest machinery and processing capacity. Planting a single variety across a large area concentrates the entire harvest into one narrow window, which is a capacity problem disguised as a simplification.
  • Disease susceptibility under local humidity and rainfall patterns.

Detail (scheduled): Almond Variety Selection in Continental and Semi-Arid Conditions

Block layout and planting sequence

Layout decisions are permanent, and they are made when the least is known about the site.

  • Row orientation balances light interception, machinery efficiency, and — on slopes — erosion control. Where these conflict on erodible ground, erosion control wins.
  • Block size trades machinery efficiency against management granularity. Very large blocks are efficient to work and difficult to manage differentially when soil or water varies across them.
  • Headlands and turning space sized for the largest machine that will ever work the block, including harvest equipment. Retrofitting turning space is expensive.
  • Road layout determining harvest logistics for the orchard's life.
  • Planting phased against infrastructure, not against nursery availability.

That last point is the one that causes the most trouble. Nursery trees arrive on a schedule set by the nursery. Irrigation gets built on a schedule set by construction. When planting follows the trees rather than the water, blocks go in before they can be irrigated properly, and first-year establishment suffers in a way that shows in the canopy for years.

Irrigation

Almonds in semi-arid conditions are entirely irrigation-dependent. Design determines yield ceiling.

Key decisions: system type and emitter layout; capacity sized to peak demand, not average; distribution uniformity as a design and maintenance target; filtration matched to water source; fertigation capability; and monitoring at more than one depth.

The design error with the longest consequences is sizing to average rather than peak demand. A system that cannot meet peak demand during nut fill produces a water deficit at the moment yield is set — every year, permanently.

See Irrigation Planning for Almond Orchards and Irrigation and Agricultural Infrastructure.

Harvest planning and machinery

Mechanical almond harvest is a chain: shake, sweep, pick up, transport, then receive and process. The chain runs at the speed of its slowest element, and the window is short.

Planning implications:

  • Capacity is calculated backward from processing throughput, not forward from orchard area
  • Harvest window length is set by variety maturity spread and weather risk
  • Transport and receiving capacity must match field output, or the field stops
  • Orchard floor condition determines harvest efficiency and product cleanliness — a decision made at establishment
  • Machinery must be maintained to work continuously through the window; a breakdown during harvest is not recoverable within the season

See Machinery Requirements for Large Almond Operations and Agricultural Mechanization.

Orchard-to-processing planning

The mismatch that catches large operations is between orchard growth and processing capacity. Orchard area expands in one step — a planting decision. Processing capacity expands in another — a capital project with a long lead time. If the orchard reaches full bearing before processing capacity is in place, the crop is sold unprocessed at the lowest margin in the chain, which is the outcome the orchard investment was meant to avoid.

Planning processing capacity against the orchard's future bearing area rather than its current one is what avoids that.

See Almond Processing and Export Development.

Preparing for European markets

EastFruit reports that Guara and Supernova plantings were designated for European export. Meeting EU requirements is a systems question, not a final-inspection question: maximum residue levels and therefore spray programme discipline, aflatoxin control through drying and storage management, traceability from block to consignment, hygiene standards in processing, and documentation sufficient to survive an audit.

Most of these are decided in the orchard and in the processing facility's design, not at the point of shipment.

This site does not claim completed and audited export shipments. Export-oriented production and variety selection for European markets are documented; delivered shipments are not. [VERIFICATION REQUIRED: export declarations, phytosanitary certificates, buyer confirmations]

See Preparing Almond Production for European Markets.

item.title: Building an Almond Processing and Export Value Chain
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
An orchard grows a crop. A value chain decides what that crop is worth. In Georgian horticulture the gap between the two has been the structural problem: producers grow well and sell unprocessed, capturing the thinnest margin in the chain while processing value is captured elsewhere.

Building processing capacity alongside the orchard was an attempt to close that gap — for the operation itself, and, as reported by EastFruit in 2021, with the stated intention of offering processing services to other Georgian almond and walnut growers.

Why processing capacity governs the orchard

Processing capacity is not a downstream detail. It sets the harvest calendar.

Almonds are harvested in a short window and must be dried to a safe moisture content quickly. If receiving and drying capacity is below field output, the field stops — or product waits in conditions where quality degrades and aflatoxin risk rises. Neither is acceptable, and the second is a food-safety failure rather than an efficiency loss.

So the planning direction runs backward: processing throughput determines harvest rate, which determines machinery and transport requirements, which determines how much area can be brought to bearing in a given year.

Getting this wrong in the other direction — orchard reaching full bearing before processing is commissioned — forces the crop out unprocessed at the lowest available margin, which defeats the purpose of the orchard investment.

Primary processing

Hulling and shelling. Removing hull and shell from the harvested nut. Throughput here is what usually defines "processing capacity" and is the constraint on receiving rate.

Drying. The critical food-safety step. Almonds must reach and hold a moisture content low enough to prevent mould growth and aflatoxin development. Drying capacity, not shelling capacity, is often the real bottleneck, and it is the one that cannot be compromised.

Cleaning and sizing. Removing foreign material, grading by calibre. European buyers specify calibre, so this determines what can be sold into which specification.

Sorting. Removing defective kernels, shell fragments and foreign material. Increasingly optical, and directly tied to achieving export grade.

Storage. Controlled conditions to hold quality between harvest and shipment. Storage capacity is what converts a harvest-time surplus into year-round sales rather than a forced sale at harvest prices.

Capacity and equipment figures are not published on this site.

My professional record includes a processing capacity of approximately 14–15 tonnes per hour, an investment of approximately USD 15 million, and a named equipment manufacturer. None of these appears here as a claim, for specific reasons:

  • The only published capacity figure is 2.5 tonnes per hour (EastFruit, September 2021) — roughly one sixth of the figure in my record. The two may be measuring different things: in-hull intake versus kernel throughput, or an initial line versus a later expansion. Until a specification sheet establishes which, publishing either number as settled would be misleading.
  • No published source isolates processing capital expenditure. Investor.ge reports GEL 150 million invested in the Udabno operation as a whole, which is a different quantity entirely.
  • Published sources spell the equipment manufacturer differently, and two real manufacturers correspond to the different spellings.

[VERIFICATION REQUIRED: equipment specification sheet, commissioning report, machine nameplate photograph, audited capital accounts]

Secondary processing

Secondary processing converts kernel into products with longer shelf life, higher value and different market channels — flour, oil, and milk among them.

The strategic argument for it: it absorbs product that does not meet whole-kernel export specification. Every orchard produces a proportion of broken, undersized or cosmetically imperfect kernel that is perfectly good food but cannot be sold as premium whole kernel. Without secondary processing that product is sold at a discount. With it, the discount becomes an input cost to a higher-value product.

That changes the economics of the whole operation, and it reduces the pressure to achieve unrealistic export-grade percentages.

Quality standards for European markets

EU market access is a systems requirement, not an inspection at the border.

  • Maximum residue levels. Determined by the orchard spray programme, years before shipment. A single non-compliant application can disqualify a consignment.
  • Aflatoxin limits. EU limits for tree nuts are strict. Control is through harvest timing, rapid drying, storage conditions and sorting — all process design, not testing.
  • Traceability. Block to consignment, documented and auditable.
  • Hygiene and HACCP in processing facility design and operation.
  • Documentation sufficient to survive an audit rather than merely to accompany a shipment.

The pattern: almost every EU requirement is met by decisions made upstream in the orchard and in the design of the facility. Very little can be fixed at the point of export.

Detail: Preparing Almond Production for European Markets

GeoGAP and commercial market access

International certification schemes such as GLOBALG.A.P. are export-oriented, expensive and demanding. Most Georgian producers cannot reach them, and those who can sell to exporters to recoup the cost. That leaves a gap on both sides: growers who want to demonstrate quality but cannot afford an international scheme, and domestic buyers willing to pay for quality with no way to verify it.

GeoGAP was created by the Georgian Farmers' Association with USAID and Chemonics support as a scaled-down, locally calibrated stepping-stone toward the international schemes. I am quoted in the Chemonics/USAID technical brief on why that matters:

"In general, we think that implementation of GeoGAP standards, and going through certification, will give farmers [the] ability to also sell their products at higher prices in the retail sector."

Chemonics / USAID Zrda Activity, A Local Certification System in Georgia, October 2021

The same brief records that Adjara Group planned to implement good agricultural practices and earn GeoGAP certification at its almond orchard, berry farm and vineyard. That is documented as a plan; this site does not claim the certification was achieved.

Detail (scheduled): GeoGAP and Commercial Market Access

Regional processing for independent growers

EastFruit reported in 2021 that management intended to offer processing services to other Georgian almond and walnut growers, with a view to a regional processing base.

This addresses the structural problem directly. An individual grower with a few hectares cannot justify hulling, drying and sorting equipment. Without access to it, the crop is sold unprocessed at the lowest margin — so the grower captures little, has no incentive to invest in quality, and the regional crop stays low value in aggregate.

Accessible regional processing changes the calculation: quality becomes worth achieving because it becomes sellable. That is a different kind of outcome from expanding one company's own orchard, and a more durable one.

Published sources record this as a stated intention. This site does not claim the service was delivered at scale, or state how many growers used it. [VERIFICATION REQUIRED: service records, grower agreements, throughput data]

item.title: Deep-Ripping and Soil Preparation for Orchard Establishment
item.dc:creator: gmetreveli
item.content:encoded:
Deep ripping is the most consequential soil operation in orchard establishment and the least reversible. Done correctly on a site that needs it, it determines the rooting volume available to a tree for the next twenty-five years. Done on the wrong site, at the wrong moisture, or in the wrong direction, it wastes substantial money and can leave the soil worse than before.

This page covers when ripping is justified, how to decide the parameters, and — the section most often missing from equipment-vendor literature — when not to do it at all.

A note on project figures. This page and its supporting articles contain no project-specific parameters — no working depths, machine horsepower, treated areas, contractor names or measured results from the orchards I have worked on. Those details are not published because the supporting documentation has not yet been reviewed. [VERIFICATION REQUIRED: dated work records, machinery specifications, soil profile descriptions, photographs]

What follows is the technical reasoning, which stands on its own and on published agronomic sources.

Why the subsoil decides an orchard's ceiling

An almond tree's productive capacity is bounded by the volume of soil its roots can occupy and extract water from. Above ground, most limitations can be managed season by season: nutrition, pests, canopy, irrigation scheduling. Below ground, almost nothing can be changed after planting.

If a dense layer sits at 40 cm, the tree has 40 cm of soil regardless of what the profile looks like below it. In a semi-arid environment that constraint compounds: a shallow rooting volume holds less water, so the tree depends entirely on irrigation frequency, which means any interruption in supply becomes a stress event rather than an inconvenience.

Deep ripping exists to remove that constraint before the trees are planted. That is its whole purpose, and it is the test for whether it is needed: is there a layer restricting root development, and will fracturing it produce a rooting volume the crop can use?

If the answer to either half is no, ripping is not indicated.

Subsoiling versus deep ripping

The terms are used interchangeably in practice, and the distinction matters because the operations have different purposes and cost profiles.

The practical difference: subsoiling addresses a problem created by farming, and recurs because the cause recurs. Deep ripping addresses a deeper restriction — often geological or from long-term consolidation — and is a one-off opportunity taken before a perennial crop goes in, because afterwards the ground is inaccessible.

Detail: Deep Ripping Versus Conventional Subsoiling

Identifying a restrictive layer

The mistake that costs the most money is ripping a site without confirming a restriction exists. The mistake that costs the most yield is not ripping a site that has one.

Both are avoided the same way: dig a pit and look.

Soil maps and survey data indicate what to expect; they do not establish what is present in a particular block. In my experience the two disagree often enough that a map should be treated as a hypothesis to test rather than a finding.

What to look for in the profile face:

  • An abrupt change in density you can feel with a knife or probe
  • Platy or massive structure where the layer above and below is crumb or blocky
  • Roots turning sideways at a consistent depth — the most direct evidence available, and it costs nothing to observe
  • Colour or mottling change indicating water perching on the layer
  • Standing water in the pit at the layer boundary after rain

Supporting measurements — a penetrometer traverse, bulk-density sampling — refine the picture. They do not replace opening the ground.

Detail: How to Identify a Restrictive Soil Layer

Soil moisture is the decision that determines success

If one thing on this page is worth remembering: soil moisture at the time of ripping matters more than depth, spacing, machine power or operator skill.

Soil fails in two modes. Dry, brittle soil fractures — cracks propagate outward and upward from the shank, and the result is a network of fissures roots can exploit. Wet, plastic soil deforms — it flows around the shank and closes behind it, and the tine polishes a smeared surface that is denser and less permeable than the layer being treated.

The second outcome is worse than not ripping. Money spent, and a new restriction created.

This is why ripping is done at the dry end of the season, when the profile is dry through the target depth — not when the calendar or the contractor's schedule suits. A site that is not dry enough should wait, even at the cost of a season.

Detail: Correct Soil Moisture for Deep Ripping

Depth, spacing and direction

Depth. Deep enough to penetrate and fracture through the restriction, and no deeper. Depth beyond the restriction consumes fuel and traction for nothing — draught rises steeply and non-linearly with depth — and can bring unsuitable material upward. The pit tells you the depth; the machine does not.

Spacing. Close enough that fracture zones from adjacent passes intersect, leaving no untreated columns between them. Fracture spreads further in dry, brittle soil than in moist soil, so spacing and moisture are a single coupled decision.

Direction. Two considerations, sometimes in tension. Ripping lines should relate sensibly to the future orchard rows, so that tree positions sit in treated ground rather than between passes. And ripping lines must not become preferential water paths down a slope — a rip line running downhill on sloping ground is a drain, and on erodible semi-arid soil it is the beginning of a gully. On slopes, ripping across the slope; where that conflicts with row orientation, the erosion risk takes precedence.

Detail: Ripping Depth, Spacing and Direction

Sequence with drainage and irrigation

Order of operations, and the reasoning:

  1. Assessment — pits, profiles, drainage evaluation
  2. Drainage — if the site needs it, install before ripping. Ripping into a site with an unresolved water table produces fractures that fill with water
  3. Deep ripping — at correct moisture, correct depth and direction
  4. Surface preparation and levelling — after the ground has settled
  5. Irrigation installation — after ripping, never before
  6. Planting

Step 5 is where expensive mistakes happen. Ripping after irrigation is installed means either destroying the system or leaving untreated strips exactly where the trees will be planted. The sequence is not flexible.

The relationship with drainage runs both ways: ripping without drainage on a site that needs both creates a network of fissures that concentrates water with nowhere to go, which is worse than either problem alone.

Detail: Deep Ripping Before Irrigation Installation

Post-ripping settlement

Ripped ground is loosened, and it will settle — through its own weight, through wetting and drying cycles, and through the first significant rainfall.

Practical consequences:

  • Do not plant into freshly ripped, unsettled ground. Trees planted before settlement end up too deep as the soil drops around them, and stem burial at the graft union causes losses that appear years later.
  • Allow a wetting cycle and a settlement period between ripping and planting. Natural rainfall is preferable; irrigation can be used to accelerate it.
  • Re-level after settlement. Surface irregularity that appears after settling affects machinery access and surface water movement for the orchard's life.
  • Expect and check for surface subsidence along rip lines.

When deep ripping should not be done

The section most often omitted. Ripping is contraindicated when:

  • There is no restrictive layer. Loosening already permeable soil achieves nothing and reduces its bearing capacity.
  • Soil is too wet. Smearing creates a worse restriction than the original.
  • The restriction is too deep to reach with available machinery — partial penetration that stops within a dense layer can worsen conditions locally.
  • The layer is a genuine barrier serving a purpose, such as a horizon perching water above saline subsoil. Fracturing it can bring salts into the root zone. On saline or sodic sites, ripping without a salinity assessment is a serious risk.
  • Subsoil material is unsuitable — strongly sodic, saline, or acidic material brought upward can be worse than the restriction.
  • Slope and erodibility make it unsafe without erosion control in place.
  • The economics do not work. Ripping is expensive in fuel, machine hours and wear. On a marginal site the same capital may do more for water infrastructure or drainage.

Detail: Common Deep-Ripping Mistakes · When Deep Ripping Can Damage Soil Structure

Cost and operational planning

Deep ripping is among the most expensive single field operations in orchard establishment. Cost drivers: depth (the dominant factor — draught rises sharply with it), soil condition and moisture, spacing, and machine and implement wear, which is substantial in stony ground.

Planning points:

  • Cost is per hectare at a given depth and spacing. Quotes that omit either are not comparable.
  • Progress rates in dry, hard ground are slower than machinery specifications suggest.
  • The narrow window when soil is dry enough is also when contractors are busiest. Book early or own the capability.
  • Budget for wear parts, not just hours.
  • Include the settlement period in the establishment timetable. It is not slack.

Quality control

Verify the work rather than assuming it. Dig a pit across the rip line after the operation and look for: actual depth achieved against specification, fracture extending laterally toward the adjacent pass, no smeared or polished surfaces, and no untreated column between passes.

Checking a small number of pits across a block, while the machine is still on site, is the difference between a specification and an outcome.
